A wearable is a piece of armour, clothing or an accessory made for one rigged character: boots, a chestplate, a hood, a cape. It comes out as its own game-ready mesh that fits the body and follows every animation. Here's how Gen Studio gets there, and why.
documents.s: How wearables, fitting and cloth work

documents.t: No open model generates a garment onto a given body mesh. The research on garments targets standard human bodies and sewn cloth, not armour on a stylised game character. What does work well: image models are good at "the same character, now wearing X"; multiview 3D models build a mesh from fixed views; fitting a mesh to a body and copying skin weights are well understood, and can be done with plain, tested code. So a wearable is made in four ordinary steps, each with takes: Design, Mesh, Fit and Skin, with an optional Paint between Fit and Skin.
documents.s: Why not just generate the piece in 3D?

documents.t: The character is rendered in its rest pose from the front, left, back and right. Qwen-Image-Edit draws the piece on each view: the front first, then the others with the designed front as a reference, so every view shows the same piece. SAM 3.1 cuts the piece out of each view by its description. Then the four masks are checked against each other. Each view's mask is compared with the shape the other three carve out in 3D, allowing for what the body hides (a boot behind a long coat). A view that disagrees is redrawn. The take shows the four views and their cut-outs, and design.json records the scores.

The Route field picks one; on Auto, the description's words decide, and failing that, the shape. Follows the body (boots, gloves, shirts, trousers): the piece is made from the body's own surface where the masks cover it, pushed out by a small clearance and given a thickness, then closed into a shell. It fits by construction. Rigid (helmets, pauldrons, belts): built in 3D from the four cut-outs with Pixal3D, a multiview model. Hanging sheet (capes): the back view's outline hung behind the body like a cloth pulled down, with folds.

A rigid piece is placed in the box its cut-outs cover, hugged onto the body by a non-rigid fit that keeps its shape, then pushed out to the clearance so the body can't poke through. A piece that follows the body only gets the push-out, as a check. fit.json records how far the fit is off and how deep the body still reaches inside. Layers stack pieces. A piece on a higher layer (a coat, layer 2) is fitted over the same character's pieces on lower layers (a shirt, layer 1). In Godot, the body under a worn piece is hidden, so it can't show through when the character moves.
documents.s: Fit: on the body, never in it

documents.t: The piece gets its skin weights from the character's own skinned body: each point of the piece copies the weights of the closest body point when their distance and direction agree, and the rest are filled in smoothly over the piece's surface (a method from a 2023 SIGGRAPH Asia paper on robust weight transfer). Each vertex gets at most four bones. This avoids the usual problems of a naive copy, such as weights bleeding from one leg to the other. The piece is exported on the character's skeleton, so it follows every clip. As a check, the character is posed (arms up, knees bent, a twist) and any body points that poke through are counted; a warning names the worst pose.

Capes, skirts, long hair and tails should swing. Gen Studio doesn't bake a cloth simulation into the clips. Instead it adds bone chains down the parts that hang, and Godot's SpringBoneSimulator3D swings them at runtime. That way the cloth reacts to whatever the character does in the game, not only to the clips you made. Which part hangs comes from the Cloth setting, or on Auto from the words: cape, skirt, robe, hair, ponytail, tail and so on. How it swings comes from the Cloth material: stiffness, drag and gravity presets for cloth, leather, hair and chain. Capsule colliders on the hips, spine, chest and thighs, scaled to the character, keep the cloth outside the body. Before a wearable's Skin take is kept, headless Godot swings the chains. If they stretch more than 5 %, the take fails with the reason. The numbers go in wear.json, and with a display a cloth.webp preview shows the swing. A character's own long hair gets the same treatment on its Rig step.
documents.s: Cloth: bone chains, swung by Godot

Two separate dials shape every result: the target look (the era you're aiming for) and the profile (how long a step may take). Keeping them apart means the same models serve a PS1-style game and a PS4-style one, and you can try ideas fast and finish them slowly without changing the look. The app says target look. The CLI, gen-project.toml and meta.json say fidelity. They're the same thing.

The target look is the era your game looks like: PS1, PS2, PS3 or PS4. It is set per project (Settings → Project → Target look, or fidelity in gen-project.toml) and sets the budgets: Target look Character triangles Prop triangles Texture Clips PS1 1,000 800 256 px 15 fps, stepped PS2 4,000 4,000 512 px 30 fps PS3 10,000 6,000 1024 px 30 fps PS4 30,000 50,000 2048 px, normal maps the clip's own rate It also sets the audio sample rate and loudness, the palettes of low-fi textures, which maps a painted texture keeps, and the preview shader. A project can change the budgets in gen-project.toml; the defaults are in Fidelity targets. It mostly changes the finishing: decimation, baking, palettes, frame rates, resampling. These are plain, deterministic code, so they are cheap and testable. The project's target look is a default. Steps that depend on it can set their own value: the Game mesh step's Triangle budget, Texture size and Normal map, a clip's frame rate. So one hero prop can have more detail than the rest. The value used is recorded in the take.

The profile picks the model and its settings: Ultra fast, Fast, Balanced or Quality. Ultra fast and Fast are for trying ideas: small, quick models, few steps. Balanced and Quality use bigger models and add finishing passes. For 2D pictures that means an upscale, a refine and a face pass. The profile can swap the model entirely. A concept at Ultra fast runs SDXL with DMD2 in 4 steps; at Quality it runs Qwen-Image at 1280 px. A Game mesh at Fast is a Blender decimate and bake; at Quality it is MeshAnything V2. The steps reference lists what each profile runs for every step. The profile is resolved in layers: the project's default, then a per-stage override in gen-project.toml ([stages.concept] profile = "quality"), then the step's own Profile field when you make a take. If a stage has no recipe at the profile you asked for (the Rig step has no Balanced one, for example), it uses the next lighter one it has, and the take records that.
documents.s: Profile: how long a step may take

documents.t: The resolver takes both dials and works out the full job: which model, with which settings, and which finishing chain with which budgets. Both values go into the take's meta.json, so a take can be remade exactly. Some pairs don't make much sense. PS4 at Ultra fast: PS4 bakes normal maps from the high poly, and ultra-fast meshes are too rough for that. PS1 at Quality: slow, for a budget of a few hundred triangles. The resolver warns about those but lets you run them. If a step runs out of GPU memory, it falls back to the next lighter profile and records that in the take (see the VRAM scheduler).

Start a project at Fast to explore shapes and sounds quickly. Retake the keepers at Balanced or Quality: the takes sit side by side, so you can compare. Pick the target look once, at the start, from the game you're making. Change it per step only for exceptions.

Gen Studio never overwrites a result. Every time a step runs, it writes a new folder. Here's what's in those folders, how the app decides which results belong together, and why every result can be made again.

An asset follows a pipeline: an ordered line of steps. A prop goes Concept → Prepped cut-out → Mesh → Game mesh, with an optional Paint at the end. A character adds a Turnaround and a Rig, then a row of steps per clip. Each run of a step makes a take, in its own folder. The app calls it Take 3, the folder is v003: <project>/assets/chest/steps/concept/v001/ v002/ v003/ steps/retopo/v001/ You use one take per step. Which one is written in the asset's canonical.json. The others stay where they are, so you can go back at any time. Using a different take changes one line, not any files. A take made from the app with Retake or New take, or with gen retake, is kept but not used until you choose it ( Use this take, or gen promote). The first take of a step is used straight away.
documents.s: A step, its takes and the one in use

documents.t: Every take records its parents: the takes in use on the step before it (and any extra inputs, such as the rig a clip is put on) at the moment it ran. If you later use a different take of a parent step, the child was made from something you no longer use. It is stale. Stale is not an error. The old results are still there and still valid for the old concept. It means "these don't match what you chose any more". A take built on another take of its step (Build on Take N, base) records that take's parents, since that's where its pixels came from, and keeps a hard link to its picture (base.png), so it still re-resolves when that take is discarded. Re-run stale leaves such a take marked: you rebuild it by hand. Re-run stale (or gen rerun-stale) makes new takes from the takes now in use, in order. If you change your mind and use the old take again, nothing is stale any more. Export refuses a stale asset. That keeps Godot from getting a character whose rig was made from one mesh and whose texture came from another.

Each take folder has its outputs (concept.png, high.glb, low.glb, sfx.ogg, …) and a meta.json with the fully resolved job: the stage, the profile and the target look it ran at, and any fallback to a lighter profile; the model, its extension and worker versions, and its weights pinned to a full 40-character Hugging Face revision; for ComfyUI steps, the workflow template's sha256 and the ComfyUI and custom-node commits; every value of the step's form, the seed, and the output of the prompt enhancer if it ran; the parent takes and their files' hashes; timings, and the licence of the model and of any imported file. Where the file format allows, the job is also embedded in the output itself (PNG text chunks, glTF extras), so a file you drag out of the folder keeps its history.

gen run --from <meta.json> re-resolves a take's job from its meta.json and checks that it comes out the same: same model revision, same template, same values. The rule in the code is simple: if a result can't be remade from its meta.json, that is a bug. A seed alone is not enough for that. A seed with a different model revision, a changed workflow template or another prompt rewrite gives a different picture. That is why everything is pinned and recorded, not only the seed. meta.json doubles as a credits log. The model's licence and an imported asset's source and licence are in every take, so you can list what your game uses.

gen.db is a SQLite index of jobs, assets and events. It makes the app fast, but it is not the source of truth: the folders are. If the database is lost or damaged, gen doctor --reindex rebuilds it from the asset folders. You can copy a project folder to another machine, open it, and every take, choice and history is there. Folders also survive tools that know nothing about Gen Studio: Godot, Blender and agents can read them directly.
Discard…, Reroll and Move to .trash (Settings → Storage → Clean up) move takes to the project's .trash/ folder. Gen Studio never deletes them. Empty .trash/ yourself when you are sure.
documents.s: Nothing is deleted behind your back

Gen Studio runs image, 3D, motion, audio and text models on one GPU. Most of these models want most of the card. The scheduler decides what is loaded, when it is swapped out, and what happens when something doesn't fit.

Every model runs in a backend: a model worker (its own process and Python environment), the managed ComfyUI, or the managed llama.cpp server. Each backend declares: a group: backends in the same exclusive group never share VRAM; its VRAM need, used for the fit badges and checked before it starts; a ttl: how many idle seconds before it is unloaded (5 minutes by default), so a batch doesn't reload a model between jobs. When a job needs a backend that isn't running, the scheduler stops the other backends in its group, then checks that enough VRAM is free before it starts the new one. The queue row says what is happening (unloading … for …, waiting for 21 GB of free VRAM), so a swap never looks like a hang.
documents.s: One heavy model at a time

documents.t: Declared needs are a starting point. Before every launch the scheduler reads the real free VRAM from the driver (NVML), because declared figures can be wrong in both directions: ComfyUI, for one, makes its usage look higher than it is. While a step runs, Gen Studio samples how much GPU memory its own processes hold. The peak is kept per stage and profile in vram.json in the data folder (the last five runs; the need is their maximum). After a step has run once on your machine, the fit badges and the scheduler use that measured number instead of the declared one. It is kept per machine, not per project, because a measurement can't be rebuilt from asset folders the way gen.db can.

If a step runs out of GPU memory, the runner queues it again one profile lighter (Quality → Balanced → Fast → Ultra fast) and says why. The take's meta.json records the chain under request.fallbacks, with each step's from, to and reason, so you can see the take was made at a lighter profile than you asked for. A step that fails even at Ultra fast fails with a plain message. If free VRAM stays too low to start at all, the scheduler waits a while, then fails with how much it needed and how much was free.

The queue prefers the job whose stage ran last. Jobs that use the same model run back to back, and the model stays loaded between them. A batch of twenty concepts followed by twenty meshes loads each model once, not twenty times.

Games, browsers and other AI tools use VRAM too. The scheduler sees them and names them in a warning (other programs are using the GPU: pid 4321 (3.2 GB)), but it never stops a process it didn't start. Close them yourself, or let the step wait. The same goes for external backends: if you point Gen Studio at your own ComfyUI or llama.cpp server in ~/.config/gen-studio/config.toml, Gen Studio starts it if a start command is set but never stops it. Its VRAM is yours to manage.

Gen Studio runs every model on your own machine, on one GPU. It doesn't call an online service to make anything. Here's why, and what it costs.

Prompts, reference pictures, imported models and every result stay on your disk. Nothing is uploaded to make an asset. The only network traffic is what you ask for: downloading models and runtimes, searching free asset libraries, and the phone page, which stays on your local network behind a token. That matters for unreleased games, for work under NDA, and for anything you'd rather not hand to a service that may train on it.

Online services change their models without telling you. A prompt that gave a good result last month may not give it today, and there is no way back. Locally, every model is pinned to an exact revision (a full 40-character Hugging Face commit), every ComfyUI workflow to its hash, and every input file to its hash. Each take's meta.json records all of it, so a take can be made again, the same, long after. gen update writes those pins into a gen.lock, and gen restore installs exactly them on another machine. See Takes, stale steps and provenance.

Once the models are downloaded, a take costs only electricity. You can make twenty concepts to find one good one, or run a batch overnight, without counting credits. Nothing waits behind other people's jobs, and nothing stops working when a service changes its terms or shuts down.
documents.s: No per-image cost, no one else's queue

documents.t: Gen Studio installs and manages what it needs under one data folder: ComfyUI at a pinned commit with pinned custom nodes, a llama.cpp server for text, one Python environment per model worker, and the weights. It doesn't depend on anything else you have set up. If you already run your own ComfyUI or llama.cpp server, you can point Gen Studio at it in ~/.config/gen-studio/config.toml; it will use it but never stop it.

Local models come with a range of licences: some fully open, some non-commercial, some with regional limits. Gen Studio records the licence of the model behind every take, and the source and licence of every free asset you import, in the take itself. It doesn't decide for you, but you can always see what your game is built from before you ship it.

Local has real costs: A capable GPU. Gen Studio is built and tested on an RTX 4090 with 24 GB. Several steps want 16 to 24 GB of graphics memory. The VRAM scheduler runs one heavy model at a time and falls back to lighter profiles, but a small card limits what you can run at Quality. Disk space. The Minimal tier is 80 GB, Recommended 266 GB, Full 358 GB, plus the environments. You can put models on another drive. A first install. Downloading runtimes and weights takes time once. Downloads resume and are checked by hash. Speed. A big hosted model may be faster per image than your card. Fast profiles keep the trying-out loop short; Quality is for the keepers.

The record in every take's meta.json of how it was made, so it can be made again. See takes and provenance.
The first picture of a prop or character, drawn for 3D.
A character drawn from the front, left, back and right, for building it in 3D.
The dense 3D model built from the concept or turnaround: Mesh on a prop, High poly on a character. An input for the Game mesh. It doesn't go in the game.
The model rebuilt within your target look's budget, with its texture baked. The Retopo step (retopo).
A model with a skeleton and skin weights, bones named for Godot's humanoid profile (skin).
A piece of clothing or armour made for one rigged character or base body, skinned to its skeleton.
A plain body (underwear, a bodysuit, a mannequin) that a wardrobe of pieces fits onto.
Where a wardrobe piece goes (feet, outer torso) and how far out (0 skin-tight to 3 outer). A piece is fitted over the lower layers.
A named set of a body's pieces (gen outfit hero travel shirt coat boots).
Bone chains down what hangs (a cape, a skirt, long hair) that Godot's spring-bone simulator swings.
A shot of an anime character in every expression, with talking and blinking frames.
A cut-out drawing split into parts on Godot bones (Skeleton2D), with idle, sway and head-tilt animations.
Several variants of one sound effect, so repeats don't sound the same.
A track split into drums, bass, vocals and the rest.
A small text model on your CPU behind the sparkle and dice buttons. See write better prompts.
The graphics card's memory. Most steps want most of it. See the VRAM scheduler.
The Model Context Protocol: how Claude Code drives Gen Studio (gen-mcp). Its tools: MCP reference.
One task per page. New to the app? Start with the tutorials.

Retake and compare: make more takes and keep the best. Reroll a take: a new seed that replaces a take. Run the stale steps: rebuild what's out of date. Add steps and paths: add a step, branch from one, delete one. Write better prompts: the writing helper, the prompt guide, your prompts and presets. Use the queue: see, pause and cancel what's running.
Retouch a picture: repaint an area you mark by hand. Vary a region: redraw one part of a concept by naming it.

Paint a model's texture: repaint it from a picture. Edit part of a model: repaint or remake only what you mark. Import your own models: bring in an FBX, OBJ, GLB, VRM or .blend. Cloth presets: make capes, skirts and long hair swing.
The mixer and layers: stack sounds and shape them. Clean up a recording: noise, clicks and a dull top end. Stems and MIDI: split a track and edit its notes.
Export to Godot: what you get, and where it goes. The Godot dock: the queue and Import inside the editor.
Batches overnight: many jobs from one file. The queue on your phone: watch and steer from the sofa.

Find free assets: search free libraries, with licences. Extensions on and off: which packs of models you have. Move your data: the data folder, and what uses the space. Libraries and drives: models on the drive you choose.
Queue many jobs from one file and let them run while you're away. A batch runs at low priority, behind anything you queue by hand.
A project: a folder with gen-project.toml. The models for the steps you'll run (gen install weights).

Make a batches/ folder in the project and write a file in it, say batches/overnight.yaml: jobs: # plain jobs, as in a job file - {asset: still, kind: prop, prompt: a copper still, seed: 1} - {asset: hero, kind: character, prompt: a young ranger in a green hood} matrix: # every combination of the list-valued fields kind: prop asset: "{prompt}_{seed}" # a name pattern prompt: [a wooden chair, a stone well, an iron lantern] seed: [1, 2] profile: [balanced] Run it from the project folder: gen batch batches/overnight.yaml The whole file is checked first: if one job is wrong, nothing is queued. Then gen batch works through the queue and reports each step as it finishes.

A matrix needs kind and an asset name pattern. Each field with a list is varied. Fields with one value are the same for every job. The example makes 3 prompts × 2 seeds = 6 props. In the pattern, {n} counts from 1, and {prompt}, {seed}, {profile} or any other field are short slugs of the value. "{prompt}_{seed}" gives a_wooden_chair_1, a_stone_well_2 and so on. Two jobs can't make the same asset name. Make the pattern include every varied field, or use {n}. Any other key goes to the steps' forms, as in a job file (slot: for a wearable, bpm: for music). The keys are in Files and steps and fields.
Run gen serve --project <project> and press Start beside the file under Batches on the phone page.

Jobs that use the same model run one after another, so the model isn't reloaded between them. If the machine crashes or you stop it, the job that was cut off goes back in the queue. gen queue run picks up where it stopped. Running gen batch again would queue the whole file a second time. A job that runs out of graphics memory is tried again one profile lighter, and the take records it.
Start small: one prompt and one seed, to check the file. Then grow the matrix. Use a fast profile for a night of ideas, then retake the best at Quality.
Use the queue The queue on your phone The VRAM scheduler

Take rumble, clicks, hiss and metallic shimmer out of a sound or track, and bring back a dull top end. Clean up is a step on Sound effect and Music assets, between the sound and its Effects. It's optional: with no Clean up take, Effects works from the sound directly. It works on made sounds and imported ones.

Open the asset and click Clean up on the rail (or add it with the +). Set Strength: Gentle, Normal (the default) or Strong. It sets how hard hiss and shimmer are cut. Strong also removes clicks from a sound effect. Set Shimmer: Auto fixes the metallic flicker generators leave in the highs, when it's measured. Off leaves it. Strong always cuts it. For a track at the Quality profile, open Advanced and say what to fix in Music repair (less reverb, clearer vocals). Leave it empty for an all-round restore. Press New take. gen retake cauldron_bubble clean --set strength=strong --set shimmer=strong gen retake dawn_theme clean --profile quality --set instruction="less reverb"

Each sound is measured first, and only what the measurements show gets fixed. Then two models can help: Model When it runs What it does FlashSR Balanced and Quality, at PS3 or PS4, when the top end is dull (under 16 kHz) Restores the missing highs at 48 kHz SonicMaster A track at Quality Repairs and masters it, following Music repair After that, the take gets the era sound and loudness as usual. The progress line says what was fixed, and clean.json in the take has every measurement.

FlashSR: if it's missing, gen install weights --group flashsr. SonicMaster is gated: accept Stability AI's licence on Hugging Face, then gen install weights --group sonicmaster. If a model isn't installed, Clean up goes on without it and says so.
On a sound effect with variants, pick the variants you want on the Clean up take before you go on. Effects uses the ones you pick. Start with Normal. Go to Strong only if hiss or clicks are left.
The mixer and layers Sound for a game Steps and fields: audio_clean

Make a cape, a skirt or long hair swing in Godot, and choose how it moves. Gen Studio adds bone chains down the parts that hang. In Godot, a SpringBoneSimulator3D swings them while the character moves. Nothing is baked into the clips, so the cloth reacts to whatever the character does in the game.

Open the character and click Rig on the rail. Set Cloth: Auto (the default) adds chains when the description mentions hair: long hair, ponytail, braid. Hair always adds them. None never does. To change how it moves, open Advanced and set Cloth material. Press Retake. Capes and skirts aren't part of the character. Make them as wearables.

Make a Wearable (under Characters & bodies in New asset), or open one. On its Design step, set Cloth: Auto reads the piece's words: cape, cloak, mantle swing as a cape; skirt, dress, robe, coat, kilt, tabard, gown as a skirt; hair, ponytail, braid as hair; tail, ribbon, scarf, tassel as a tail. Or pick Cape, Skirt, Hair, Tail or None. Set Cloth material under Advanced if Auto isn't right. Run the pipeline to Skin. The chains are added and checked there.
documents.s: A cape, skirt or coat as a wearable

documents.t: Material Stiffness Drag Gravity For cloth 0.6 0.4 1.0 capes, skirts leather 1.4 0.5 0.8 coats, belts hair 0.9 0.3 0.6 hair, tails chain 0.4 0.2 1.6 chains, heavy jewellery Stiffness springs the chain back to its rest shape, drag damps the swing, gravity pulls it down. Auto uses cloth for capes and skirts, hair for hair and tails. gen retake herbalist skin --set cloth=hair --set cloth_material=chain gen retake red_cape wear_design --set cloth=cape --set cloth_material=leather

A wearable's Skin take swings the chains in headless Godot before it's kept. If they stretch more than 5 %, the take fails and says why. With a display, the take also has a cloth.webp preview of the swing. The numbers are in wear.json under cloth_check. Export writes a <piece>.cloth.json beside the wearable, and for a character's own hair a <name>.cloth.json and a ready <name>_cloth.tscn.

In Godot, Wearables.cloth() sets up the simulator from a .cloth.json (see Godot scripts). Capsule colliders on the hips, spine, chest and thighs, scaled to the character, keep the cloth out of the body.
How wearables, fitting and cloth work A base body and an outfit

See Gen Studio's queue and import finished assets from inside the Godot editor. The dock is a small editor plug-in. It shows and imports, and makes nothing itself. It talks to gen serve on your machine.
A Godot 4 project (a folder with project.godot). A Gen Studio project with some finished assets.

Install the dock into the Godot project: gen dock install ~/games/my-game It copies the add-on into addons/gen_studio/ and turns it on in project.godot. Start the server for your Gen Studio project, and leave it running: gen serve --project ~/gen/my-game-assets Open (or reopen) the game in Godot. The Gen Studio dock appears and says Connected. The dock has two lists, refreshed every few seconds (or press Refresh): Queue: what is running and waiting. The status line says (paused) when the queue is paused. Assets: each asset with its kind, marked stale when a step needs a rerun. Press Import beside an asset. Its files are copied into res://assets/gen/<asset>/, the same as Export to Godot, and Godot imports them.

Both commands use port 8765 by default. If you change it, use the same one for both: gen serve --port 9000 and gen dock install ~/games/my-game --port 9000. The dock keeps the server's address and token in addons/gen_studio/server.json. The token stays the same across restarts, so you install the dock once. Don't commit server.json to a public repository: the token lets anyone on your network use the queue.

"gen serve: not reachable at …": start gen serve, or check the port matches. "… is not a Godot project": point gen dock install at the folder that holds project.godot. Import refuses a stale asset: run its stale steps first. The dock doesn't show after install: reopen the project in Godot, or turn on Gen Studio under Project Settings → Plugins.
Export to Godot The queue on your phone: the same server, from your phone.

Mark a part of a 3D model in the viewer, then repaint or remake only that part. Everything outside it stays as it was: the same vertices, the same triangles, the same skin. Use it to fix a hand, swap a gauntlet or a helmet, add a piece (a pauldron, a handle), or repaint one glove.
You need a model take: Mesh, Game mesh, Rig or Paint. Repaint needs a concept or a reference picture. Replace and Attach need gen.qwen-edit, gen.trellis2 and gen.concept.

Open the model's step, press Open large (the inspector), and press Select part. Mark the part: Click it. Each click is a point SAM 3.1 looks for on four views of the model. Alt+click marks what is not the part. Shift+drag brushes over it, and every face under the brush is taken as it is. [ and ] change the brush's size. Right-drag turns the view, middle-drag pans, the wheel zooms. Undo takes back the last mark, Clear starts again. Press Edit part…. An Edit part step is added after this one (on a new path when the step already has a next step) and opens with the part filled in, built from the take you marked. On a take of an Edit part step it's the next pass instead: New take opens, starting from that take, so edits stack. Set the step: Mode: Repaint paints the part's texture again and keeps its shape. Replace remakes the part in 3D and joins it in its place. Attach makes a new piece there, as its own mesh. What it should become: "a red leather glove", "an iron ring handle". Empty: the same part, sharper. Or name it: words for the part instead of clicks ("the left glove"). Press Generate. The take shows the found part tinted orange (Painted region) beside the result.

Mode Takes about What happens Repaint 1.5 min Paint runs on the whole model, then bakes onto the part's faces only, feathered at the edge. With a prompt, Qwen-Image first redraws the part Replace 6 min Four views framed on the part are redrawn, cut out and built in 3D. The old faces go, and the new part is joined with a boolean union. Only a narrow seam may change Attach 6 min The same, but the new piece stays its own mesh and the model stays whole On a rig, the new vertices get skin weights from the body around them, so the part moves with the skeleton. part_edit.json beside the take records what happened, including a hash of the faces that had to stay, before and after. They match.

One part at a time for Replace. A selection in two pieces remakes the larger. Click the middle of the part. A click on a glove often finds the forearm too; Alt+click the forearm to leave it out, or brush. A part the body hides (an armpit, the inside of a hand) is the weak spot. Brush it.

gen branch knight skin part_edit gen retake knight b1/part_edit --set selection=.edits/knight/skin/selection-1a2b3c4d5e6f.json \ --set mode=replace --set "prompt=a steel gauntlet with five separate fingers" gen retake knight b1/part_edit --set "region=the left glove" --set mode=repaint \ --set "prompt=a red leather glove" selection is a JSON file the app writes for you: {"points": [{"p": [x, y, z], "n": [...], "sign": 1}], "brush": [{"p": [x, y, z], "r": 0.03}]}, in the model's own (glTF) space, rest pose.
Paint a model's texture Steps and fields: part_edit
Copy an asset's finished result into your Godot project, ready to use.
A Godot 4 project: a folder with project.godot. The asset's steps finished, with no stale ones. Export refuses a stale asset, so Godot never gets a half-updated model. Run the stale steps first.

Open the asset. Press Export to Godot in the toolbar. The first time, pick your Godot project's folder. Gen Studio remembers it. Shift-click Export to Godot to pick another. Export to Godot on Home does every finished asset that isn't stale, at once. gen export copper_still ~/games/my-game gen export herbalist ~/games/my-game --project ~/gen/my-game-assets

Files land in res://assets/gen/<asset>/, and shared scripts such as wearables.gd in res://assets/gen/. Export copies the takes in use: Asset Files Prop the Game mesh .glb; a toon scene when the project's toon look is on Character the rig .glb with every clip inside (Godot loops the *_loop clips); <name>.cloth.json and <name>_cloth.tscn when it has hair chains Wearable the .glb, .wardrobe.json, .cloth.json, and wardrobe.gd / wearables.gd Base body outfits.json and wardrobe.gd beside the body Texture its maps and a material.tres Effect the sprite sheet and its materials Sound, music .ogg with loop points (or WAV or FLAC) Dialogue Dialogue Manager files Anime set, 2D rig sprite_frames.tres, portrait.gd, Ren'Py files; the 2D rig's .tscn and its parts What the scripts do is in Godot scripts.

In Settings → Project: Toon look in Godot: off for standard shading. On for cel shading and an outline, which adds a scene that puts the toon shader on every mesh. Export sounds and tracks as: OGG (small), WAV (24-bit, the loop in its smpl chunk) or FLAC (lossless, loop tags). Press Save in the Sound group.

Export again after a retake. The files are replaced in place, so scenes that use them pick up the change. To drag one file instead, use the handle at the bottom right of any output frame: drop it into Godot, Blender or a folder. "is not a Godot project": pick the folder that holds project.godot, not a subfolder. "has nothing to export yet": run the asset's steps first.
The Godot dock: import from inside the editor. Godot scripts

Turn a pack of models on or off, so its steps, asset kinds and downloads appear or go away. Most of Gen Studio's steps come from extensions: packs of steps, each with its own models and settings (gen.concept for concept art, gen.ace-step for music). Most are on. The anime pack, gen.anime, its add-on gen.anime-noobai and the pixel art and chiptune pack, gen.pixel, ship off.

Open Settings (Ctrl+,) → Extensions. Search, or filter by category. Each row has a switch and its library, size on disk and description. Pick one to see its steps and models. Click the switch. Restart the app. Changes apply on the next start. If you turned one on, install its models under Settings → Models. Or don't: they download the first time a step needs them, after the app asks.

gen ext list # every extension, on or off, and its stages gen ext enable gen.anime gen install weights --group anime gen ext disable gen.anime The switches are stored in the [extensions] table of ~/.config/gen-studio/config.toml.

An off extension adds nothing: no steps, no asset kinds, no fields, no downloads. Assets you made with it keep their folders and takes, but they stay out of the app until you turn the pack back on. Turning a pack off deletes nothing.

An add-on offers another model for its parent's steps. gen.anime-noobai adds models to the anime pack's steps. It's active only while its parent is on, and the step then shows a Model choice beside Profile.

Put an extension folder in extensions/ of the Gen Studio folder, or in <data folder>/extensions/. gen new extension me.foley --kind worker scaffolds one. gen ext validate checks every installed manifest, pin and environment; gen ext validate <folder> checks one. How to write one is in the repository's AGENTS.md. Every installed extension has a page in the wiki.
Turn off packs you don't use, to keep Settings → Models and New asset short. gen update writes gen.lock from the installed extensions. gen restore installs exactly what it pins on another machine.
Libraries and drives: models take space. Profiles and target looks
Search free libraries for models, textures, sounds, music, shaders and voices, and import one as an asset with its licence.

Kind Libraries Models Poly Haven, ambientCG, Sketchfab, OpenGameArt Textures Poly Haven, ambientCG Sounds Openverse (Freesound), OpenGameArt Music Openverse, OpenGameArt Shaders Godot Shaders Voices AivisHub (Japanese voices) If one library is down, the others still answer.

Open Find free assets: the magnifier beside New asset on the Assets page, File → Find free assets…, or New asset → Free online assets. Pick a Kind. Type what you want (wooden chair, rain on a window) and press Search. Each result shows its source and licence. Press Listen to hear a sound, music or voice, or Open page to see it in your browser. Press the import button: Prop or Character for a model, Import for the rest. The asset opens like one you made. Its first take is the imported file, and the licence and source are in its meta.json.

gen find "wooden chair" gen find "brick wall" --textures gen find "rain on a window" --sounds gen find "calm village" --music gen find "dissolve" --shaders gen find "calm" --voices gen import polyhaven:brick_wall_001 --as texture gen import openverse:<id> --as sfx --asset rain_loop gen find prints each result's name (source:id), title and licence. gen import <name> --as prop|character|texture|sfx|music|shader|voice brings one in.

Sketchfab downloads need your API token, in ~/.config/gen-studio/config.toml. Without it, Sketchfab results show only Open page. [assets] sketchfab_token = "your token" Some results can't be downloaded directly (gen find adds open and the page). Download those yourself, then import the file. An AivisHub voice is pinned by its file's sha256, so it can't change under you. Check the licence before you ship. CC0 needs nothing, CC-BY needs a credit. Gen Studio records it and doesn't decide for you. An imported sound goes through Clean up and Effects like a made one.
Import your own models Clean up a recording
Bring in a model you have as a prop or character, so you can paint it, rig it, give it clips and export it like a made one. Supported files: FBX, OBJ, GLB and glTF, VRM, and Blender's .blend.
Blender must be installed and on your PATH. It converts the file.

The quickest way: drop the file on Home's prompt bar. Or: File → Import a model…, or New asset → A 3D model under From a file. Pick Character model or Prop model. Fill in Asset name (lower-case letters, digits, _ and -). In Model file, pick the file. In Licence, say where it comes from and its licence (CC0, bought on a store). It's kept with the take. Leave your own for your own work. Press Generate.

gen import my_knight.fbx --as character gen import crate.blend --as prop --asset old_crate gen import ~/models/lamp.glb --as prop --licence "CC-BY 4.0, Jane Doe" Without --asset, the name comes from the file name.

Blender converts the file to one GLB, which becomes the asset's Game mesh take, and renders a front view, which becomes a Concept take. You can vary or restyle that render like any concept. A prop is ready to paint and export. A rigged humanoid gets its Rig take straight away. Its bones are mapped to Godot's humanoid names, so clips work at once. An unrigged character runs the Rig step next. The model is kept as it is: its triangles aren't cut down to the target look's budget.
"Blender is not on PATH": install Blender, or put it on your PATH, then retake the step.
Find free assets: a free model imports the same way. Paint a model's texture: give it a new look. Steps and fields: import_model

Keep each extension's models on the drive you choose, and move them later. It works like Steam's library folders. A library is a folder on any drive where models and their environments live. Your data folder is the first library, Data folder. Add a library on another drive, and you can install an extension there or move one there later. Nothing is tied to one drive.

Open Settings (Ctrl+,) → Storage. Under Libraries, press Add library… and pick a folder on the drive. Check the drive, its filesystem and free space, give it a name (e.g. Games SSD), and press OK. Gen Studio makes a gen-studio-library folder there, with a small library.json that names it. gen library add /mnt/games --label "Games SSD" gen library list Make default on a library sends new extensions there. Some drives (exFAT or FAT USB sticks) can't hold environments: such a library shows Models only, and those extensions keep their environments in the Data folder.

When a step needs a model that isn't installed, the prompt says Downloads to · N GB free. Change… lists your libraries with their free space. For an extension that isn't placed anywhere yet, the one you pick becomes its library. For one that already lives on another library, choose Just this download (only this model goes there) or Move there too (the move runs first, then the download). Setup's Where models go step does the same for everything at once: pick a drive, and a library is made there at Install.

Settings → Extensions, pick the extension; its Storage group shows which library it is in and how much it takes. Press Move…, pick a library. Each one says whether it fits ("37 GB fits · 140 GB left after") or how much it is short. Choose what happens to the old copy: Keep the old copy in the trash (the default), or Delete the old copy, which asks you in red first. Press Move. The progress shows in the Storage group; Cancel keeps what was copied, and Move… again carries on from there. Every model file is checked by its sha256 before anything switches. Environments are rebuilt from their lockfiles on the new drive, not copied. If a model is shared with another extension (e.g. the text encoder of both Wan models), it moves too, and the other extension reads it from the new drive. The dialog says so. gen ext move gen.vfx "Games SSD" # old copy to the library's .trash/ gen ext move gen.vfx "Games SSD" --delete-old # asks first; --yes doesn't gen install weights --group vfx-video-14b --library "Games SSD"

Its library shows Drive missing, and so do its extensions. A step that needs it says which drive to connect, e.g. "… uses gen.vfx, which is on "Games SSD" (/mnt/games), and that drive isn't connected. Connect it and press Retry." Nothing is downloaded again in the meantime. Plug it back in at the same place and everything works again. You don't need to restart (the app checks every 10 s). If it mounts somewhere else now, press Relocate… on its row (or gen library add <new place>). It is found by its library.json, keeps its name, and the links are updated.
Remove… only forgets the library; nothing on the drive is deleted. It is greyed out while extensions or files are still there: move them first.

gen doctor lists each library (free space, whether it is connected) and checks every link: links to a missing drive; files that are on a library other than where their extension is placed; leftovers nothing uses; foreign links, which point into a folder that is no library (e.g. models you moved by hand). Fix them with gen library add <folder on that drive> --adopt, which moves those files into the library instantly. If the links get lost (a broken move, a reinstall), gen doctor --relink rebuilds them from the libraries.
Move your data: the Data folder itself, with the runtimes and gen.db. Extensions on and off

Split a track into parts, write a new part under the same song, and edit the notes as MIDI. Both are optional steps on a Music asset. They never run by themselves: add them with the + on the rail. A sound effect or effect can have a MIDI step too.

Open the track and press the + on the rail. Pick Stems. Press New take. You get drums, bass, vocals and the rest. Each stem can be soloed or muted. New take on a stem writes a new part under the same song: a new bass line, say.
Add MIDI, with the + on the rail. Press New take. It writes a MIDI file of each stem, and a preview of the song played with General MIDI instruments.

Press Edit MIDI on a MIDI take. Channels (left): one row per stem, with its instrument under it. Drums: a Pattern of 16 steps a bar, a lane per drum. Everything else: a Piano roll, with a Velocity lane under it. Snap runs from 1/4 to 1/16. Timing tools, above the grid: Line up with the beat, Snap to audio, Quantize (with Strength, Swing and Ends), and Clean up (with Legato). Play renders your edit and plays it. Save changes the take you opened, and steps after it are marked stale. The take as it was goes to the project's .trash folder.
gen add-step dawn_theme music stems gen run-to dawn_theme stems gen run-to dawn_theme midi # adds and runs what it needs on the way
Sound for a game The mixer and layers

Stack other sounds under a sound effect, run it through a rack of effects, and save the result as a take. What you hear is live: there's no render step until you save. The mixer is the centre of a sound's or track's Effects step.
You need a Sound effect or Music asset whose first step has a take in use (see Sound for a game).
Open the asset and click Effects on the rail (or add it with the +). Pick the New take card in the strip. Or, to start from a take, pick it and press Edit in the mixer.

Press Add layer… and pick where it comes from: one of the project's sounds, listed by name; Find a match…: the project's sounds, each with the part it would fill; From a file…: a sound file you have; Generate a layer…: describe it (a deep sub-bass thump) and press Generate. It makes a new Sound effect asset as long as this sound. Pick a variant there, then add it here. Suggest layers asks the writing helper for ideas. On each layer row, set: the part it fills: Full, Transient (the first 80 ms, the snap), Body, Low end or Tail; Gain, Pan and Pitch; where it starts: drag it along the lane, or press Align to line its attack up with the sound's. Press S on a layer to hear it alone. The light at the left of a row turns the layer off. A new layer starts 6 dB under, lined up with the sound's attack.

For a quick start, open Quick setup in the inputs. Pick plain choices (Tone, Body, Punch, Character, Room, Amount) and press Fill the rack, or type a description in Describe it (distant, metallic, in a cave) and press From the words. Start from… loads a ready-made rack. Press Add effect… to add a slot by hand. Effects are grouped by what they do: EQ and filters, Dynamics, Distortion, Modulation, Delay, Reverb, Pitch and time, Multi-effect, Utility, Your plugins. VST3 plugins in ~/.vst3, /usr/lib/vst3 or /usr/local/lib/vst3 are listed too. Pick a slot to see its settings on the right, as knobs and faders. A plugin has Plugin window, for its own interface. Each slot has a light (on and off), a wet/dry knob, and a ⋯ menu with settings, move, duplicate and remove. Drag the grip to reorder. The bypass button over the slots plays the sound without the rack, at the same loudness, so you can compare. Compare on the transport shows the input as a ghost behind the waveform.

Press New take. The layers and rack are rendered into a new take, at the loudness its Role sets. From the command line, the rack is a JSON value of the chain field: gen retake cauldron_bubble effects --set role=ambience --set loop=true

Role sets the loudness and whether the sound is mono (placed in 3D) or stereo. Channels overrides that. Turn on Seamless loop for ambiences: the end cross-fades into the start. Every take records the settings of each slot, so a take made with Quick setup can be remade exactly.
Clean up a recording: fix noise before the effects. Steps and fields: audio_fx

Move Gen Studio's data folder to a bigger disk, see what uses the space, and reuse model files you already have. The data folder holds the model weights, the worker environments, the managed ComfyUI and llama.cpp, caches and gen.db. It's ~/.local/share/gen-studio/ by default and can grow past 100 GB. Your projects live elsewhere and aren't moved. To keep only the models on another drive, use libraries instead. It's the simpler choice for most people.
An empty folder on the new disk, with room for everything (check with What uses the space below). Nothing running: let the queue finish or pause it.

Open Settings (Ctrl+,) and pick Storage. Under Data folder, press Move… and pick the empty folder. Wait for it to finish. It copies everything, checks every file arrived at its size, then leaves a link at the old path, so every setting keeps working. When it says Moved, it shows where the old copy is (renamed <old>.moved-<time>). Delete that copy yourself once everything works. Settings → Storage. From the command line: gen data move /mnt/bigdisk/gen-studio To move it back, run gen data move with the original path: the link is replaced by the real folder.

What uses the space on the Storage page (or gen data usage) lists, biggest first: each extension's weights, each project, caches, runtimes, worker environments, and weight files no installed extension names (orphans). Remove beside weights deletes those model files. Steps that need them won't run until you install them again. Remove beside a cache is safe: it is rebuilt as you use the app.

If you downloaded some weights before (for ComfyUI, say), Gen Studio can use them instead of downloading again. Press Import model files… on the Storage page and pick the folder that holds them. Every file whose size and sha256 match a pinned weight is linked (or copied) into place. gen data import ~/ComfyUI/models
documents.s: Reuse model files you already have

documents.t: Under Clean up → Old takes (the last group on the Storage page), Gen Studio counts the takes in this project that are not in use, not favourites, and over 14 days old. Move to .trash moves them to the project's .trash/. Nothing is deleted until you empty .trash/ yourself.

To start with the data folder somewhere else, set data_dir in ~/.config/gen-studio/config.toml before the first install. The uv cache (~/.cache/uv) is separate and can be large too; it isn't moved. After a move, gen doctor checks the disk, GPU and runtimes.
Libraries and drives: each extension on the drive you choose. Extensions on and off: turning off a pack you don't use stops its downloads. Why local
Repaint a model's texture from a picture with Hunyuan3D-Paint, then bake it onto the game mesh. The mesh, its UVs and its rig stay as they are.

A prop or character with a Game mesh take, made or imported. About 21 GB of free graphics memory, and 4 to 7 minutes. Paint is one of the heaviest steps. The Paint model's weights. If they're missing, the app asks before it downloads them. Hunyuan3D-Paint has a non-commercial licence that excludes the EU, the UK and South Korea. Gen Studio records it in the take.

Open the asset. Press Run next: Paint on the Game mesh, or add Paint with the + on the rail. It's optional, and Run to end skips it. Leave Reference image empty to paint from the concept in use (and, for a character, its turnaround). Or pick your own picture. Press New take. The take is the game mesh with the new texture. On a character, the Rig step is built from the painted mesh, so it turns stale if it already ran.

In Only paint, name the part as you'd point at it: the face, the boots. With a part named, Build on Take N paints on that take, so parts stack; a whole repaint starts from the step before. Lower Paint strength below 1 to keep some of the model's own texture under the paint. Press New take. The rest keeps its texture. To mark the part by hand in 3D, use Edit part of a model.

This is how to give an imported model a new look. Click Concept on the rail and pick a take (for an imported model, its render). Press Restyle…, describe the look in What it should look like (a weathered bronze knight) and press Restyle. You get a new concept take with the same outline. Use that take, then run Paint. From the command line, to paint another take of the Game mesh or the Rig as a new take of that same step: gen retake knight concept --set control=renders/knight.png --prompt "a weathered bronze knight" gen retake knight retopo --set paint_from=2 gen retake knight skin --set paint_from=1 --set region="the boots" --set mix=0.7 paint_from names the take to paint. image, region and mix are the form's fields.

New maps baked onto your mesh's own UVs. Which ones depends on the target look: base colour at PS1 and PS2, plus roughness at PS3, plus metallic at PS4. At PS1 and PS2 the base colour also gets a palette, the same readability pass as the original texture.

"Paint needs a Game mesh take first": run the steps up to Game mesh. Out of memory: close other GPU programs. It looks wrong from behind: the concept shows only the front. Characters use their turnaround too; for a prop, give it a reference picture that shows more.
Edit part of a model Vary a region Import your own models Steps and fields: paint
The rail shows only the steps an asset has. Add the next one, try another route from any step, or delete what you don't need.

Press the dashed + at the end of a row on the rail. Add step lists what can follow, under headings (Edit, Make 3D, Rig and motion, Animate, Sound, Text, Shader), each with what it does, the model it runs at this profile and about how long it takes. The first card, marked Recommended, is the step the asset's template runs next. Pick one, and its form opens. A download icon beside its time means its model isn't installed yet: the app asks before it downloads. Run next in the bar above a take does the same for the recommended step, and runs it.

A branch is another route from the same step, kept beside the first. Use it to try a different finish without losing the one you have. Hover a pill and press the small + under it. Or right-click it → Branch from here…. Pick the step. The new path is a row of its own on the rail, named b1, b2 and so on. It has its own takes and steps, and each row has its own colour. gen branch still retopo paint gen retake still b1/paint To build the next step from an older take without a new path, right-click the take → Build next step from this take.
Right-click an optional step → Skip this step. It's drawn dashed and dimmed, and the steps after it build as if it weren't there.

Right-click it → Delete step…. It lists what goes with it: the step, the steps after it on its path, and any paths and clips leaving from those, each with its take count. Everything moves to the project's .trash/. You can't delete an asset's first step. gen delete-step still paint
gen add-step still retopo paint # after Game mesh gen run-to still paint
documents.s: Add a step on the command line

documents.t: Run the stale steps Takes, stale steps and provenance

Watch the queue, pause it, start a batch and pick new takes from your phone while the machine works. The page runs on your own machine and is reachable only on your local network. Nothing goes through the internet.
Your phone and the Gen Studio machine on the same network (Wi-Fi or LAN). A Gen Studio project. For batches, YAML files in its batches/ folder (see Batches overnight).

On the Gen Studio machine, start the server for the project: gen serve --project ~/gen/my-game-assets It prints a line like Gen Studio on your phone: http://192.168.1.20:8765/?t=…. Open that whole URL on your phone. The ?t=… part is the token; without it the page refuses every request. Bookmark it: the token stays the same across restarts. Use the page's three sections: Queue: what is running and waiting. Pause stops new jobs from starting; Resume starts them again. Waiting for a choice: takes newer than the one in use, per asset and step. Use makes one the take in use, as Use this take does in the app. Batches: the files in the project's batches/ folder. Start queues one at low priority and starts working through the queue. Press Ctrl+C on the machine to stop the server.

gen serve --project ~/gen/my-game-assets --port 9000 # another port (default 8765) gen serve --project ~/gen/my-game-assets --host 127.0.0.1 # this machine only The default host, 0.0.0.0, makes the page reachable from your network.

Keep gen serve running while you use the page. Stopping it closes the page; jobs already running go on. Using a take from the phone marks the steps after it stale, as in the app. Rerun them later from the app or with gen rerun-stale <asset>. The token lives in the data folder. Anyone with the full URL on your network can use the page, so don't share it.

The page doesn't load: check both devices are on the same network, and that a firewall on the machine allows the port. "open the URL gen serve printed (it has the token)": open the full URL with its ?t=… part.
Batches overnight The Godot dock: the same server, inside the Godot editor. A clip from your phone: a different thing, motion capture from a video.
Each model wants a prompt written its own way. Gen Studio has four things to help: the writing helper, the prompt guide, your saved prompts, and presets for everything else.

A small model that runs on your CPU, so it never takes the GPU. It answers in about two seconds. It's on prompt fields and name fields: Sparkle on a prompt: rewrites what you wrote the way this step's model wants it. Dice on an empty prompt: a new prompt in the style of the guide's examples. Sparkle on a name: a name from the prompt, unique in the project. An undo arrow puts back what you had. Some steps also have Enhance the prompt. That's different: a larger text model rewrites the prompt when the step runs, and the rewrite is saved with the take.

Press (i) beside a prompt. The guide has a tab per model, the profile's model first: a summary, the structure it likes, tips, what to avoid, your prompts and examples. Use fills the field. Every step's guide is also on its wiki page, under Tips.
Press the star beside a prompt to save it for that stage. It shows in the guide under your prompts. Delete it there.

For the rest of a form: open Advanced, press Save as preset, and name it. Use fills the form from it, for that stage in every project. A step with no take yet starts from the values you used last for that stage.

Say what it is, what it's made of and how worn it is. Gen Studio adds the camera and background a step needs, so leave those out. One thing per prompt. A table with a lamp on it makes one fused piece. Change one thing per take, so you know what made the difference.
Retake and compare Vary a region

See what's running and what's waiting, pause it, and cancel or retry a job. One big model fits on the GPU at a time, so jobs wait their turn. Everything you start goes in the queue, across all your projects. Downloads have a lane of their own beside the GPU job.

The status bar, at the bottom, shows the running job and its progress, then CPU, RAM, GPU and graphics memory. Queue at its right end opens the list. Each row links to its step. Home's On the GPU shows the running job, what's next and what's holding the memory. Rows run newest first, so the running job is at the bottom.
Press Pause in the queue's header. The running job finishes, and nothing new starts. Resume starts them again.
Hover a row. Cancel stops a queued or running job, and Retry starts a failed or cancelled one again. To cancel everything a step has going, right-click it on the rail → Cancel its runs.

The row and the step's failure panel say what went wrong in plain words, and what to do. Retake tries again, Copy log copies the job's log. A job that runs out of graphics memory goes again one profile lighter by itself, and the take says so: "Fell back: ran at Fast". See the VRAM scheduler.
A job that finishes or fails while the window is in the background sends a desktop notification.
gen queue run # work through queued jobs without the app
Batches overnight The queue on your phone Troubleshooting

Replace a take with a new seed, without adding another take to the strip. Use it when a take is close but has one bad roll (a broken hand, a muddy sound) and you don't want to keep the bad one. To keep both, make a new take instead.

Open the asset and click the step on the rail. Right-click the take in the strip. Choose Reroll (replace this take). The step runs again with a new seed. The new take goes where the old one was. If the old take was in use, the new one is used instead, and the steps after it turn stale.
gen reroll still concept # the take in use gen reroll still concept 2 # Take 2 (v002)

Its pictures are copied into the new take's rerolls/ folder, so you can flip back to them. The old take, with its other files, goes to the project's .trash/. Nothing is deleted. Empty .trash/ yourself when you're sure.
Reroll changes only the seed. To change the prompt or a slider, use Retake. The new take has its own seed in its meta.json, so it stays reproducible.
Retake and compare Run the stale steps
Make more takes of a step, look at them side by side, and choose the one the next step uses.
You need an asset whose step has run at least once (see your first prop).

Open the asset and click the step on the rail. Change what you want in the inputs on the left: the prompt, the Profile, a slider. Leave them for the same settings with a new seed. Press Retake under the inputs (R). On the New take card in the strip, the same button reads New take. The new take appears in the strip while it runs. The take in use stays in use, so nothing after it changes yet. Each take gets a new random seed while the shuffle button beside Seed is on. Turn it off to set your own. To start a take without opening the step, right-click the step on the rail and choose Retake.

Hover a take card and tick the box in its corner, or Ctrl-click it. Pick two or more. Press Compare N in the step's title bar. Compare shows the same output of each take side by side, with its stats. 3D views turn and zoom together. Sounds stop the others when one plays, and they're already matched in loudness, so you compare the sound and not the level.

Click a take, then Use this take in the title bar (U). When there's a step after it, the button reads Use and run and starts that step too; its small arrow opens Run next, which goes on from the take already in use. Hover a take in the strip and press its check mark, or double-click it, to use it without running on (also right-click → Use this take). The steps built from the old take are now stale.

gen retake still concept --prompt "a copper still with a tall thin neck" gen retake still retopo --set triangles=2000 --profile balanced gen status still # every step's takes, the one in use, stale steps gen promote still concept 3 # use Take 3 (v003) --set takes any field of the step's form by its key (the keys are in steps and fields). A take from gen retake is kept, but not used until you promote it.

Change one thing per take. Then you know what made the difference. Right-click a take for Favourite and a rating from 1 to 5, to find good ones later. Discard… moves a take you don't want to the project's .trash/. You can't discard the take in use. gen discard still concept 2 does the same. Advanced under the inputs shows what the profile runs, and has Save as preset for values you reuse.
Reroll a take: a new seed that replaces a take instead of adding one. Run the stale steps Takes, stale steps and provenance

Repaint an area you mark by hand, and keep every other pixel. Erase parts of a Rim light or Relight take the same way. Use it to fix a hand or a face, to change one part ("make the cape red"), or to keep only the good parts of a rim light.
You need a picture take: a concept, an anime image or shot, a texture, any step that makes a picture. It must be the one in use.

Open the picture's step and show the take you want to fix. Press Retouch… in the title bar. A Retouch step is added after this one and opens. If the step already has a next step, it goes on a new path. In the panel on the right, press Draw the area… and paint over what to repaint. It opens on the picture you're about to change: on New take, what Starts from says (the step before's take, by default); on a take, that take. Press Apply, then set the step: Model: Same as the picture redraws with the model that drew it. Qwen-Image-Edit 2511 changes the area by an instruction instead. Strength: 0.3 to 0.5 keeps the shape and colour and fixes detail. 0.5 to 0.7 reinterprets. 1.0 draws it anew from what's around it. Prompt is the picture's own, filled in. With Qwen, write The change ("make the cape red"). Press New take.

Pick a take: everything in the panel now works on it, and changing a field stays on that take. Build on Take 2 starts a new take from Take 2's picture, so fixes stack: Take 1 fixes the hand, Take 2 the face. The area stays, with Clear beside it, since you often go over the same spot. Retake repeats Take 2's settings from where Take 2 started, to try that pass again. It keeps the seed unless you change it or turn on the random seed. On New take, Starts from picks the picture it starts from, shown large with the area on it: Original by default, or any take. The two small previews show the Original and the take this one was built on. Click one to open it in the big view. If the concept changes under a stack, the takes are marked stale and stay that way until you rebuild them. Fix hands and Fix face (Preset) find each hand or the face and redraw it up close, with nothing to draw.

Tool Key What it does Brush B Paint the area. Set size ([ and ], or Ctrl + wheel) and hardness Eraser E Paint it away Lasso, Box L, R Fill a shape Click K SAM 3.1 finds the part you click. Alt-click cuts, drag for a box Find by name SAM 3.1 finds the part you name The wheel zooms at the cursor, middle-drag or Space-drag pans, Ctrl+Z undoes. Hold \ to see the picture without the area. Click and Find by name need ComfyUI running, which any job starts.

On a Rim light or Relight take, press Erase parts…. Paint over the light you don't want. The picture before the step shows through. The eraser paints the light back. Press Make the take. It's made on your CPU in a second or two, without running the model. Stack them: a FlowEdit Rim light for the soft outer rim, a Qwen Rim light after it, then erase what Qwen overdid.
documents.s: Erase parts of a Rim light or Relight

documents.t: gen branch still concept retouch gen retake still b1/retouch --set mask=hand.png --set strength=0.5 gen retake still b1/retouch --set mask=hand.png --set "model=Qwen-Image-Edit 2511" \ --set "change=make the base iron" gen retake still b1/retouch --set mask=face.png --set base=2 # from Take 2 gen retake rin anime_rim --set erase=too_much.png --set erase_from=3 mask and erase are 8-bit PNGs at the picture's size (white: repaint or erase, grey: partly, black: keep), relative to the project.

Mark a little past the part. Grow and Soft edge (under Advanced) blend it in, and nothing outside the mark changes. Not what you wanted? Reroll for another seed. A colour a shade off? Match colour (on by default) shifts the repaint to the colours around it.
Vary a region: the same idea on a concept, by name only. Retake and compare Steps and fields: retouch

The first time you open Gen Studio, a Set up Gen Studio window opens over the app. Make a few choices, and it downloads what it needs in the background while you use the app. Each kind of asset works as soon as its models arrive.

Linux and an NVIDIA GPU. Gen Studio is built and tested on an RTX 4090 with 24 GB. Many steps want 16 to 24 GB of graphics memory; smaller cards can run the Fast profile and fall back when a step doesn't fit. With no NVIDIA GPU, you can point it at a ComfyUI on another machine. Disk space. 80 GB for the Minimal tier, 266 GB for Recommended, 358 GB for Full. The setup window shows the exact plan per drive before anything downloads. Godot 4, for your game. Blender on your PATH. The game mesh step, Paint and importing models use it. gen doctor says whether it's found. uv, to install. While Kasumi, the app's UI framework, is a private repository, installing also needs SSH access to it on GitHub.
packaging/install.sh # from a checkout: installs gen, gen-app and gen-mcp gen-app # opens the app and the setup window There's also an AUR package, packaging/aur/PKGBUILD.

The steps are on the left, and you can go back to any of them. The plan, under them, shows where models go, the tier, the packs, what downloads and how much room is left. It changes as you choose. Welcome: Express takes the suggestion for this machine and goes straight to the plan. Custom shows every step. Not now closes the window; Home then shows a Finish setup row. System check: the GPU and its memory, the driver and CUDA, RAM, each drive's free space, uv and Hugging Face. It never stops you. It says which profile new assets start at: Balanced from 20 GB of graphics memory, else Fast. Where models go: one row per drive, with what the plan needs against its free space. Your data folder stays where it is. Pick another drive and the models go to a library there. Choose folder… picks any folder. What to install: the tier, Minimal (props and characters at Fast), Recommended (every kind at Fast and Ultra fast) or Full (every profile). Then the packs: 3D, Audio, Effects, Text and LLM, Anime (off by default) and Gated models. An unticked pack isn't switched off: its models download the first time you use them, after the app asks. Import models: model folders you already have (ComfyUI's models/, the Hugging Face cache, Stability Matrix, LM Studio). Ticked files are checked by sha256 and linked, so they aren't downloaded again. Skip if you have none. Install: queues the work: imports, ComfyUI, the model environments, llama.cpp, then each pack's models. Each is a row with its progress, and they carry on after a restart. Continue in background closes the window. Ready: each pack is ready, downloading, queued, on first use or off. Make a first prop opens New asset.
Settings → Setup → Open setup reopens the window. Install then queues only what's new: a pack you ticked, a bigger tier, models on another drive. To remove models, use Settings → Models.

gen setup # the same questions, the suggestion as the default gen setup --express --yes # take the suggestion and install gen setup --tier minimal --packs 3d,audio --library /mnt/games --dry-run # the plan and sizes only gen setup --status # per pack: ready, downloading, on first use gen setup --resume # queue again what failed gen doctor # check the GPU, driver, disk and runtimes gen setup follows the downloads until they finish. Ctrl-C stops following; the jobs stay queued, and the app or gen queue run carries on.
A tour of the app, then your first prop.

Rebuild the steps that were made from a take you no longer use. A step is stale when a take it was made from is no longer in use. Say you use concept Take 3 instead of Take 1: the Prepped cut-out, Mesh and Game mesh were made from Take 1, so they're stale until they run again. Stale isn't an error. The old results are still there.

On the rail, stale steps have the stale colour. The step's title bar says stale: and what changed. Home's Waiting for you has a card for it, and Assets has a Stale filter. gen status still lists them.
Open the asset. Press Re-run stale in the toolbar. It only shows when something is stale. Each stale step runs again from the takes now in use, in order. Each makes a new take, and that take is used.

A take made with Build on Take N (a stack of Retouch or Edit passes, say) gets its picture from that other take, not from the step before. Running it again would keep the old pixels, so Re-run stale and Run to here leave it, and the steps after it, marked: the title bar says rebuild by hand. To rebuild one, start from New take on that step, with Starts from set to Original, and make the passes again. Or use the old take of the step before again, and the mark goes.

Run to end runs every step that's missing or stale, to the end or the next review. Right-click a step → Run to here rebuilds up to that one only. Auto-continue makes a finished step start the next one by itself, up to the next review. It's set per project.
gen rerun-stale still # every stale step, a character's clips too gen run-to still retopo # only up to the Game mesh
Export to Godot refuses a stale asset, so Godot never gets a half-updated model. Liked the old result better? Use the old take again, and the steps after it aren't stale any more.
Retake and compare Takes, stale steps and provenance

Change one part of a concept picture by naming it, and keep every other pixel. Use it when a concept is right except for one thing: the handle, a sleeve, the colour of a cloak. It's faster than retaking until the whole picture comes out right. To mark the area by hand, or to fix a picture that isn't a concept, use Retouch.

Open the asset, click Concept on the rail, and click the take you want to change. Press Vary region… in the title bar. In What to change, name the part as you'd point at it: the handle, the left sleeve. In Change it to, say what it should become: a twisted iron handle, a torn red sleeve. Press Vary. SAM 3.1 finds the part you named, and only that part is redrawn. The result is a new take. The take you varied stays as it was.

gen retake still concept --set vary_from=2 --set region="the handle" \ --prompt "a twisted iron handle" vary_from is the take to change. Add --set grow=32 to let the redraw reach further past the part's edge (16 pixels by default) so it blends in.

Keep the region short and concrete. The helmet works better than the thing on his head. Describe only the new part in Change it to, not the whole picture. See a seam at the edge? Retake with a larger grow. To change the whole look but keep the outline, use Restyle… (see Paint a model's texture). Then use the varied take, and run the stale steps so the model is made from it.
Retouch a picture Retake and compare
Facts, generated from the code so they can't go stale. Look things up here.
Facts, generated from the code so they can't go stale. Look things up here.
Everything the app does, and more, from a terminal. Run it from a project folder, or pass --project. Each command's help is below, as gen --help prints it.

What each target look (fidelity in files and on the CLI) sets by default. A project can override the budgets in gen-project.toml ([budgets.prop], [budgets.character]); a take can set its own triangles and texture on the Game mesh step.
The files you can write by hand: a project, a job, an extension's manifest.
What Export copies into res://assets/gen/, and their functions.
What kind: in a job file makes, and the steps it runs, by their ids. In the app these are in New asset; the wiki has a page for each.
What Claude Code (or another MCP client) can call on gen-mcp --project .
Every pinned weights file, by extension and group (gen install weights --group ), with its exact revision and licence. Licences are recorded in each take that uses them.
The app's keys. Help → Keyboard shortcuts shows them too. Text fields keep their own keys.
Every step a pipeline can run by its id, the model each profile uses, and its form. The keys go after --set on the CLI. The wiki has the same steps with tips.

Everything the app does, and more, from a terminal. Run it from a project folder, or pass --project. Each command's help is below, as gen <command> --help prints it. usage: gen [-h] [--version] {setup,doctor,run,make,mcp,serve,dock,batch,import,find,status,outfit,promote,retake,reroll,run-to,add-step,branch,rerun-stale,discard,delete-step,export,install,ext,library,data,queue,new,update,restore} ... Gen Studio positional arguments: {setup,doctor,run,make,mcp,serve,dock,batch,import,find,status,outfit,promote,retake,reroll,run-to,add-step,branch,rerun-stale,discard,delete-step,export,install,ext,library,data,queue,new,update,restore} setup set up Gen Studio: folder, tier, packs, imports, then install doctor check Python, uv, GPU, driver, disk and ComfyUI run run a job file through the slice, or check a meta.json make quick job without a file, e.g. gen make prop "an oak barrel" mcp Claude Code: add the MCP server and the gen-studio skill serve the queue on your phone (LAN page with a token) dock the Gen Studio dock in a Godot project (talks to gen serve) batch queue many jobs from one file (jobs and a matrix) import bring in a model you have (fbx, obj, glb, vrm, blend) find search free models, textures, sounds, music, shaders and voices status an asset's step versions, canonical ones and stale steps outfit save a base body's named set of wardrobe pieces promote make a candidate version of a step canonical retake one more take of a step (kept until you promote it) reroll a new seed for a take, replacing it (the old one's pictures kept in rerolls/) run-to build or refresh an asset's steps up to this one add-step add a step after the last one of a path branch start a new path from any step (b<n>/<stage>) rerun-stale refresh every stale step of an asset, clips too discard move a take that isn't in use to the project's .trash delete-step move a step, the steps after it and paths from them to .trash export copy an asset's finished result into a Godot project install install a managed runtime or model weights ext list or validate extensions library library folders: where models and envs live data the data folder: move it, see what uses the space, import queue work through queued jobs new scaffold a new extension update write gen.lock from the installed extensions and runtimes restore install and verify exactly what gen.lock pins options: -h, --help show this help message and exit --version show program's version number and exit

usage: gen add-step [-h] [--project PROJECT] asset after stage positional arguments: asset after the step it follows: the end of the main path or of a b<n> path stage what it runs, e.g. image_to_mesh (gen ext list shows stages) options: -h, --help show this help message and exit --project PROJECT
usage: gen batch [-h] batch_file positional arguments: batch_file options: -h, --help show this help message and exit

usage: gen branch [-h] [--project PROJECT] asset step stage positional arguments: asset step the step the new path starts from stage the new path's first step, e.g. reframe options: -h, --help show this help message and exit --project PROJECT

usage: gen data [-h] {move,usage,import} ... positional arguments: {move,usage,import} move copy the data folder to <path>, verify, then symlink usage space used by weights, projects, caches, envs, orphans import bring model files you already have, matched by sha256 options: -h, --help show this help message and exit
usage: gen delete-step [-h] [--yes] [--project PROJECT] asset step positional arguments: asset step options: -h, --help show this help message and exit --yes don't ask --project PROJECT

usage: gen discard [-h] [--yes] [--project PROJECT] asset step version positional arguments: asset step version e.g. 2 or v002 options: -h, --help show this help message and exit --yes don't ask --project PROJECT
