What Export copies into res://assets/gen/, and their functions.

Gen Studio wardrobe (spec 016): dress a base body at runtime. Each piece's .glb has a .wardrobe.json beside it (its slot, layer, the body vertices it covers and its cloth chains); outfits.json beside the body names sets of pieces. Wardrobe.equip($Body, "res://assets/gen/coat/coat.glb") Wardrobe.unequip($Body, "torso_outer") Wardrobe.wear_outfit($Body, "res://assets/gen/hero/outfits.json", "travel") One piece per slot is worn; putting one on takes off what was in its slot. The body under what's worn is hidden (its triangles left out), so it can't poke through. static func worn(character: Node) -> Dictionary: What a character wears: slot -> {"path", "info"} (kept on the character as meta). static func equip(character: Node, piece_path: String) -> void static func unequip(character: Node, slot: String) -> void static func wear_outfit(character: Node, outfits_path: String, outfit: String) -> void

Gen Studio wearables (spec 011): put a piece on a character at runtime. The piece's .glb shares the character's skeleton (same bone names and rest pose), so its meshes move onto the character's Skeleton3D and follow every animation. Wearables.wear($Knight, preload("res://assets/gen/leather_boots/leather_boots.glb")) Wearables.remove($Knight, "leather_boots") A piece with cloth chains (spec 014: a cape, a skirt) brings its extra bones, and the .cloth.json beside it sets up a SpringBoneSimulator3D on the skeleton: one setting per chain, its material's stiffness, drag and gravity, capsule colliders on the body. A character's own chains (its long hair) come from its .cloth.json the same way: Wearables.cloth($Girl, "res://assets/gen/girl/girl.cloth.json") (the exported _cloth.tscn already does this). static func wear(character: Node, piece: PackedScene) -> Array[MeshInstance3D]: Instance piece and move its meshes onto character's skeleton; returns them. static func cloth(character: Node, path: String) -> void: Set up the simulator for a character's own chains (its hair) from its .cloth.json. static func remove(character: Node, piece_name: String) -> void: Take off a piece put on with wear() (by its scene's name).

A Gen Studio sprite or portrait set: put this on an AnimatedSprite2D whose sprite_frames is the set's sprite_frames.tres. Each expression is an animation; "_talk" flaps the mouth and "_blink" closes the eyes, which happens by itself every few seconds. func show_expression(name: String) -> void func talk(on: bool) -> void

Gen Studio toon look: on load, every MeshInstance3D under this node gets toon.gdshader with its own albedo (texture and colour) and outline.gdshader as the next pass. Rigs and clips keep animating (only materials change). func apply(node: Node) -> void

What Claude Code (or another MCP client) can call on gen-mcp --project <game>.

Add a step that runs stage after the step after (see next_steps); returns its key. branch starts a new path there (b/): the main path stays as it is, use it for an edit you may not keep or when after already has a next step. Adding in line a stage the template doesn't have takes the template's remaining steps off the path, so it's refused unless you pass branch or inline. To run it: fields, then retake. Arguments: name, after, stage, branch, inline
Give another character the same motion: clip of source becomes the clip name of target, retargeted onto its rig. Arguments: source, clip, target, name

An asset's graph: steps lists every step, also those not run yet, with its key (what you pass to other tools; stage is what runs: the key skin runs the stage rig), state (done, stale, queued, running, failed, not started), after, takes and the take in use. A gate step waits for your review; run_to carries on. b/... are paths from a step, clips//... a character's clips. Arguments: name
Cancel a job: a queued one at once, a running one at its next check (and the steps queued after it). Arguments: job_id

Godot 4.7's import checks on the takes in use (or one step's): a game mesh imports, a rig has its bones and skinned meshes, a clip its length, loop and drift, a shader compiles; plus what the steps measured (turnaround sides, wearable view agreement, the body poking through a piece). Problems are listed; an empty list means all is well. Arguments: name, step
Takes of a step side by side in one labelled image (default: all, at most 6), each shown by its first picture; the text lists them as look does. Arguments: name, step, versions

Take a step away, with the steps after it on its row and the paths from them: to the project's .trash, never deleted outright. Without confirm it only reports what would go; tell the user before you confirm. Arguments: name, step, confirm
Move a take that isn't in use to the project's .trash. Without confirm it only says what it would do. Arguments: name, step, version, confirm

Copy an asset's finished result into a Godot project (assets/gen//). It reads the last step on the main path that makes the asset's kind of result, a step you added included; step names another, e.g. the end of a path (b1/retouch). The reply says which it read. Arguments: name, godot_project, step

A step's form, whether it has run or not: each field (label, type, default, choices, descriptions, help) with its value in use, the profiles and models it can run with and what each would download, and also: arguments outside the form. retake takes all of them. stage alone gives a stage's form before you add it (from next_steps). Arguments: name, step, stage

Search free assets online: kind is model, texture, sound, music, shader or voice. Each result has its uri, licence and page; bring one in with make(kind="import_prop" (or import_character, import_texture, import_sfx, import_music, import_shader, import_voice), asset, fields={"model" for models, else "source": uri, "licence": ...}). Arguments: query, kind

How a stage works: page is its wiki page (what it does, what it runs, how long, its fields); models its prompt guide where it has one (summary, structure, tips, what to avoid and examples, per model and profile). next_steps and asset give the stage ids. Arguments: stage

Download weights groups (the group of a refusal's needs) as a queue row beside the GPU job, to where the user's libraries place them. Ask the user first and say the size: without confirm this only reports the size. Arguments: groups, confirm
A job's status (queued, running, done, failed, cancelled), phase, progress and error; when done, its result files. Arguments: job_id
The queue, every project's since the GPU is shared: active (running and queued, with asset, step, phase and progress) and failed (recent failures with their errors). Arguments: limit

What can be made: each kind's steps (key is what you pass, stage what runs; gate stops a chain for review, manual you start yourself), its first form, extras a job can take beyond it. Advanced fields are by name: fields(stage=...) has them whole. off: packs that are off, and the command for the user to run. Arguments: none

See a take (default: the one in use): pictures as images with their sizes, a model as a labelled sheet of four views, a clip or video as frames, a sound as a waveform, text inline. grid draws a labelled 10 % grid on each, for reading positions for make_mask and select_part (as fractions, x then y, from the top left). Arguments: name, step, version, grid

Queue a new asset of kind (see kinds) named asset (lowercase, a-z0-9_-) with its form fields, e.g. {"prompt": "an oak barrel", "profile": "fast"}; extras in kinds go there too (a clip's clip). A model that isn't installed is refused with its size unless on_missing is "install" (ask the user first) or "fast". Returns the queued job ids. Arguments: kind, asset, fields, on_missing

Draw a mask for Retouch's mask or Erase's erase, at the picture's exact size. step is the Retouch step (it draws on the picture before it) or the Rim light, Relight or other step whose take you mean (version, default in use). shapes is a list of {box: [left, top, right, bottom]} or {polygon: [[x, y], ...]}, as fractions of the picture; look with grid=true helps you read them. soft feathers the edge, in pixels. Returns the path to pass as the field and a picture of the area in red: check it before you run. Naming the area with Retouch's find is usually better than drawing it. Arguments: name, step, shapes, version, invert, soft

What can follow a step (the app's Add step, Branch from here): fits lists each stage with what it does, its group, seconds, the model at the project's profile, the download it needs, and recommended for the template's next; not_now lists those that can't, and why. Then fields(stage=...), add_step, and retake to run it. Arguments: name, step
Save a base body's named set of wardrobe pieces (wearable assets made for it); export writes it to outfits.json. Arguments: body, name, pieces
Which round-robin variants of a sound take go on to Clean up and Effects (an empty list: all of them). The steps after it go stale. Arguments: name, step, version, names
The project: its target look (ps1 to ps4), default profile, triangle and texture budgets, audio format, and each asset with its kind and the last step that has a take. Arguments: none
A new seed for a take (default: the one in use), the same settings, replacing it when done; its old pictures stay in rerolls/, the old take goes to .trash. Arguments: name, step, version
Refresh every stale step of an asset, its clips too. Arguments: name

Run a step with these values: another take, or a step's first (a new step's first take is used by itself; later ones wait for use). Takes any field of fields(name, step) plus its also arguments; unset ones keep their last values (the reply shows them; null clears one). on_missing as for make. Arguments: name, step, fields, on_missing

Your verdict on a take waiting for review (job says needs_review; with [agent] judge = "agent" the local model doesn't judge): accept it or not, with notes. It goes into the take's judge.json and notes; use it, or submit a fix as a new take. Arguments: name, step, accept, notes, version

Queue an asset's missing or stale steps up to step (a key from asset), as one chain (the app's Run to end); with only_stale, refresh stale steps without building missing ones. on_missing as for make. Arguments: name, step, only_stale, on_missing

Mark a part of a mesh or rig take for Edit part's selection, as the viewer's Select part does. Each click is {view: "front"|"left"|"back"|"right", x, y, sign}: x and y are fractions within that panel of look's four-view sheet (grid=true helps), sign 1 for the part, -1 for what isn't. With brush (a share of the model's size, e.g. 0.05) each click marks the faces around it directly; without it the job's SAM 3.1 grows a click into the part. Blender on the CPU, a few seconds. Returns the path to pass as selection and the views with what the clicks hit tinted. Naming the part with region is usually better than clicking. Arguments: name, step, clicks, version, brush

The machine, read-only: packs on and off, weights by install tier with sizes, library folders with free space, first-run setup, and the doctor's failures. Agents don't change these: for_the_user_to_run names the commands to pass on. Arguments: none

Hand in a file you made (a fixed .gdshader, an edited PNG, a .glb), or a result from a path (a retouched picture back to its concept), as a new take of a step: it replaces one output (output, default the first) of take version (default the one in use), the rest is copied, and the take records "agent: claude-code". It isn't used until you use it. A Retouch mask isn't a take: make_mask writes it, the step's mask field reads it. Arguments: name, step, file, output, version, note
A step's takes, oldest first: version, in use, seed, profile, prompt, the form values asked for, rating and favourite, and its files. Arguments: name, step
Make take version of a step the one in use (later steps then show as stale). Arguments: name, step, version
Block until a job ends (done, failed, cancelled) or timeout_s passes, then report it as job does; call it again while the status is still queued or running. Arguments: job_id, timeout_s

Every pinned weights file, by extension and group (gen install weights --group <group>), with its exact revision and licence. Licences are recorded in each take that uses them. Tier (spec 027): gen install weights installs Minimal and Recommended (--tier minimal only the first, --tier full On demand too). An On demand model downloads the first time a step needs it, after the app asks; By name ones only with --group. Tiers are worked out from the recipes, with every pack's default settings (the anime pack's groups count when it is on). How it moves motion longtext What happens over time: 'bursts outward, then the flames curl up and fade to smoke' Loop loop bool False For fire, auras and steady effects: the last frames blend into the first Length (seconds) duration float 1.0…5.0 2 How long the effect lasts, up to 5 s (what the video model draws in one pass). Longer takes longer to make: 5 s is about 2.5 times 2 s. The flipbook keeps up to 64 frames at PS4, more below. Blend blend choice (add, alpha) add How the effect is drawn over the game: Add for glow and fire, Mix for smoke and dust. (advanced)

One piece at a time. Character character text The character asset (it needs its Rig step). Slot slot choice (auto, head, hair, face, neck, torso_inner, torso_outer, hands, waist, legs, feet, back, accessory) auto Where it goes in the character's wardrobe: one piece per slot and layer is worn at a time. Layer layer choice (auto, 0, 1, 2, 3) auto A piece is fitted over the same character's pieces on lower layers: a coat (2) over a shirt (1). (advanced) Clearance (metres) clearance float 0.0…0.05 0.008 How far off the body the piece sits after it's pushed out. (advanced) Cloth cloth choice (auto, none, cape, skirt, hair, tail) auto Bone chains down the parts that hang, so they swing in Godot. Auto reads the piece's words (cape, skirt, coat, robe, scarf...). Cloth material cloth_material choice (auto, cloth, leather, hair, chain) auto How it swings: stiffness, drag and gravity for Godot's spring bones. (advanced)

Built into the core (no model). Field Type Default What it does Route route choice (auto, conforming, rigid, sheet) auto Follows the body: boots, gloves, shirts, trousers are made from the body's own surface, so they fit by construction. Rigid: helmets, pauldrons, belts are built in 3D from the four views, then fitted. Hanging sheet: a cape, its outline from the back view, hung behind the body. Auto picks a sheet for a cape, else by how far the piece stands off the body. Thickness thickness float 0.0…0.05 0.0 How thick a piece that follows the body is, in metres (0: 0.6 % of the character's height) (advanced)
Five screens and four words. Read this once, then make your first prop.

An asset is one thing you make: a prop, a character, a sound. A step is one stage of making it: Concept, Turnaround, Game mesh. An asset is a row of steps. A take is one try at a step. Takes stay until you discard them. The take in use is the one the next step builds from. Change the take in use, and the steps built from the old one turn stale: still there, but out of date. One click rebuilds them.

The app opens here. It answers "what's happening, and what needs me?" The prompt bar makes something straight away. Pick a kind, write a line, pick a profile, press Make it. All kinds… opens the full list. You can also drop a picture, a model or a sound on it to import that file. Latest takes are the newest result of each asset. Waiting for you lists what can't go on without you: failures, reviews, stale steps, and finished assets not yet in Godot. Each card has its fix. On the GPU shows the running job, what's next and what's using the graphics memory. Projects switches between your games. A project is a folder.

Every asset in the project. Press Assets in the top bar, or Ctrl+2. The left side filters: by group, or by Needs you, Working, Stale, Favourites and Not exported. Click a card to see its steps on the right, double-click to open it. The bar under each card has one segment per step, in the step's status colour.

Ctrl+N, or All kinds… on Home, or New asset on the Assets page. Two questions: what do you start from, and what is it? From a description makes something new. From a file brings in what you have: a picture, a model, a sound, a shader, or free assets from online libraries. The form on the right shows the steps the kind runs, so you see the path before you start.

This is where the work happens. Each open asset is a tab in the top bar. From the top: The toolbar: the name, Export to Godot, Auto-continue and Run to end. Re-run stale shows when something is stale. The rail: the steps, as pills. A dot shows each one's status. Click one to open it. An asset made from another one (a Shot from its Character) starts with that asset, marked source: its picture to look at, nothing to change there. The dashed + adds a step. Right-click for more: retake, run to here, branch, delete. Inputs (left): what the step builds from, then its form. The profile, the prompt, the settings. Advanced has the rest. Retake at the bottom makes a new take. The tool panel (right, on steps that change something you already have): small previews of what the take came from, this take's tools (on Retouch: the area, find by name, the change), and Build on Take N and Retake. Details folds up at its foot. The take (middle): large. Double-click, or Open large, for the big viewer. The bar above it has the take's tools, and Run next or Go to for the next step. Takes strip (bottom): every take of this step, oldest first. The last card, New take, shows what it starts from, or on a first step the last take for reference. Details (right, on steps with no tool panel): model, seed, time, licence: how this take was made. By default a new asset runs its first step, then waits. You look at the takes, keep one, and press Run next. Run to end does the rest in one go. Auto-continue runs on by itself until a step that needs review.

The bottom bar shows the running job and how busy the machine is. Queue, at its right end, opens the list of what's running and what's waiting. One big model runs at a time, so jobs wait their turn. See the queue.

Settings at the top right, or Ctrl+,. Models: what's installed, what fits your GPU, and install or remove. Project: this game's Target look (PS1 to PS4), default profile, and sound levels. Storage: where things live, and what uses the space. Extensions: packs of models and steps, on and off. Appearance: colours, text size, Reduce motion. Setup: the first-run window again. About: the version, the machine check, licences.

Two settings shape every result, and they're separate on purpose: Target look is the era your game looks like, PS1 to PS4. It sets the polygon and texture budgets. Profile is how long a step may take, Ultra fast to Quality. It picks the model. More in profiles and target looks.

Ctrl+K searches every action and asset. On an asset, [ and ] move between steps, ← and → between takes, R makes a new take, U uses the picked take. F1 opens help on the step you're on. All of them: keyboard shortcuts.
Each problem: what you see, why, and what to do.

Why: the model didn't fit beside what else uses the GPU: a game, a browser with hardware video, another model. Do: close what else uses the GPU, or retake at a lighter profile. Home's On the GPU shows what's holding the memory. A step that can falls back to the next lighter profile by itself and says so on the take ("Fell back: ran at Fast").
documents.s: A step failed: "Ran out of GPU memory"

documents.t: Why: that step's model hasn't been downloaded. The default install leaves out models only Balanced or Quality use. A download icon beside a profile or an Add step card says so before you pick it. Do: in the app, press Download and run (it queues the download, then the step) or Run at Fast. In a terminal, run the command the message gives: gen install weights --group <group>. The models reference lists the groups. gen install weights --tier full fetches every on-demand model at once.

Too dark or flat: the export uses the baked texture. At PS1 and PS2 it's palette-reduced on purpose. Faces inside out: retake the Game mesh step. It's a bug; please report the asset. Too many polygons: the budget comes from the target look. Set the Game mesh step's Triangle budget, or the project's [budgets].
documents.s: The model looks wrong in Godot

documents.t: Thin parts (a chair's legs, a still's stand) are what goes first. Retake Mesh at Balanced or Quality. Or fix the concept: a clean, simple shape builds better.
documents.s: Parts are missing from a model

documents.t: The Turnaround step warns when it can't tell. Retake it. The 3D model needs fixed 90° views.
documents.s: A character's left and right are swapped

documents.t: Clips stay in place by default; check the job file doesn't set in_place: false. For motion capture, film side-on with the whole body in frame.
documents.s: A clip slides, or the feet float

documents.t: Raise Clearance and run on from Fit. For a piece over another, check the lower piece was made first. wear.json in the take lists the poke per test pose.
documents.s: A wearable pokes through the body

documents.t: Doesn't move: the piece's words didn't name a hanging kind. Set Cloth to cape, skirt or hair. Too floppy or stiff: change Cloth material (see cloth presets). cloth_check in wear.json shows the swing and stretch measured in Godot.
Turn the pack on in Settings → Extensions → gen.anime, restart the app, then gen install weights --group anime.
The step says which drive to connect. Plug it back in; the app checks every 10 seconds. If it mounts somewhere else now, see libraries and drives.
Stale steps: run them first. "is not a Godot project": pick the folder that holds project.godot.
gen doctor checks Python, the GPU and driver, disk space and the runtimes. A failed job's panel has its log (Copy log).

Learn by doing, start to finish. Each one ends with something in your game. New here? Do them in this order. Your first propYou'll make a copper still: concept art, a 3D model, a game mesh, then put it in Godot. About 10 minutes on a 24 GB GPU, most of it waiting for the models. A character, from concept to GodotA herbalist with a rig and a walk cycle, in Godot. About 15 minutes at the Fast profile. A clip from your phoneFilm yourself doing a move, and put it on your character. About 5 minutes, plus filming. Sound for a gameA sound effect, a few voiced lines and a looping theme for one small scene: a herbalist's shop. About 10 minutes. A shader from a descriptionDescribe a shader in a sentence and get a .gdshader that compiles in Godot, with sliders for what you want to tweak. About 2 minutes at Fast. A base body and an outfitDress one body in many outfits, and swap them at runtime in Godot. About an hour at Fast for the body and four pieces; most of that is the model and rig steps. An anime character with sprites and a 2D rigRin, the elf on these pages, was made this way. Define a character once, take shots of her, then make a visual novel sprite set and a 2D rig for Godot. About 30 minutes without the LoRA, about an hour with it. Working with Claude Code over MCPClaude Code can run Gen Studio for you: make assets, look at the takes, pick, retake and export.

Rin, the elf on these pages, was made this way. Define a character once, take shots of her, then make a visual novel sprite set and a 2D rig for Godot. About 30 minutes without the LoRA, about an hour with it.
documents.s: An anime character with sprites and a 2D rig

documents.t: The anime pack is off by default. Turn it on in Settings → Extensions → gen.anime, restart the app, and install its models: gen install weights --group anime

Press All kinds…, then Anime character under Anime. Describe them in Danbooru tags: who they are, hair, eyes, build and outfit. Rin's are: 1girl, solo, elf, pointy ears, blonde hair, very long hair, black eyepatch, red eyes, mole under mouth, burgundy vest, sleeveless, white fur collar, grey turtleneck, black belt, dark brown shorts, black gloves, brown thigh boots You get a full-body sheet on white: the definition every shot copies.

Tags keep a character close, not exact. The optional LoRA step trains a small add-on for the drawing model on pictures of her. It takes 20 to 40 minutes and the whole GPU. Every shot of her uses it from then on. Rin's was trained on 120 of 320 pictures, the ones that matched her design.

Make a Shot of a character (under Anime): pick the character, a Framing (knee-up is the usual sprite), a Pose, and a Background: Transparent for a sprite, or A scene. Write the rest in Shot: smile, looking at viewer, or sitting, reading book, library. Up to four characters fit in one shot. With three or more, each is redrawn in its own place (Layout), so they don't swap clothes.

The optional Rim light step after a shot paints a bright, thin rim on the edges facing a light, like fighting-game key art. Pick the Rim colour, Light from and Strength (1 to 5). Keep only the rim colour drops anything else the relight painted. The take shows the lit picture, the raw relight and the cut-out. The result changes with the seed. If the rim is faint, Reroll the take. About one in four or five is a great rim. gen retake rin_wave anime_rim --set strength=3 --set filter=true gen reroll rin_wave anime_rim

Make a Sprite or portrait set from the knee-up shot: every expression you ask for, each with talking and blinking frames, a faceset, and files for Ren'Py (.rpy) and Godot (sprite_frames.tres with portrait.gd).

Make a 2D rig (cut-out animation) from the same transparent shot. It's split into parts (hair, face, arms, legs, torso), the hidden areas are filled in, and you get a Godot scene with bones and three animations: idle breathing, a sway and a head tilt. The back hair swings. Open <name>.tscn in Godot. The AnimationPlayer plays idle on start.
A character defined once, then shot in any framing. Her own LoRA for an exact look. The rim light, sprite sets and 2D rigs.
A herbalist with a rig and a walk cycle, in Godot. About 15 minutes at the Fast profile.
documents.s: A character, from concept to Godot

documents.t: Do your first prop first. This tutorial uses the same project, takes and export.

Press All kinds… on Home, then 3D game character under Characters & bodies. Write: a young herbalist woman in a patched green wool coat, leather satchel at her hip, tall brown boots, braided red hair, no hat Press Generate. Or: gen make character "a young herbalist woman in a patched green wool coat, leather satchel at her hip, tall brown boots, braided red hair, no hat" --asset herbalist The concept is drawn in an A-pose with the arms away from the body, so it builds cleanly in 3D. Keep held things out of it: a sword fused to a hand can't be rigged. Make it a prop.

Press Run next: Turnaround. It draws the front, left, back and right from the concept. Check two things. Left and right aren't swapped (a warning tells you when it can't tell). And all four show the same character. If one view is wrong, press Retake; the steps after it wait for the take you use.

Press Run to end: High poly builds the dense model from the four views. Game mesh fits your target look's budget. Rig adds a skeleton and skin weights, with bones named for Godot's humanoid profile. Rig stops for review. Open it large and play the test poses: arms up, knees bent, a twist. If a joint is off, move it in the joint editor and retake with Keep the skeleton. Do this before you make clips; fixing a joint later means retargeting them again. Long hair or a cape? The Rig step's Cloth setting (Auto) adds bone chains down long hair, so it swings in Godot. See cloth presets. Capes are wearables. Press Continue when the rig looks right.

Press New clip in the toolbar. Name it walk, write a person walks forward at a steady pace, then press Generate. Or use a video of yourself: see a clip from your phone. The clip is put on the rig at your target look's frame rate, looping and in place. It has its own row on the rail. A job file can turn those off with loop: false and in_place: false. From the command line, a job file: # walk.yaml asset: herbalist kind: motion clip: walk prompt: a person walks forward at a steady pace gen run walk.yaml
Press Export to Godot and open the .glb: the clips are in its AnimationPlayer. A character with hair chains also gets <name>_cloth.tscn, the model with Godot's spring-bone simulator set up.
A character's steps: concept, turnaround, mesh, game mesh, rig. Reviewing a rig before going on. Clips, from text or video. Next: a clip from your phone, or a base body and an outfit.

Claude Code can run Gen Studio for you: make assets, look at the takes, pick, retake and export. gen mcp install --project ~/your-game This adds the gen-studio MCP server at user scope and the gen-studio skill. In a new Claude Code session, ask: make a wooden barrel, show me two takes of the concept, use the better one and export it to ~/godot-game. It can do what the app does: run steps, add a Retouch or an Edit part step, try another path, and say what it saw. What it uses: make, wait, job: start and follow jobs; look, compare: see takes as pictures (four views of a model, frames of a clip, a sound's waveform); asset, next_steps, add_step, fields, retake, use, run_to: the step graph; make_mask, select_part: the area to retouch or the part to edit, when naming it isn't enough; check, export: Godot's import checks, then the export. It asks you before a download. It can only move steps and takes to the project's .trash, and it leaves extensions and library folders to you: it tells you the command. For several games, gen mcp install --scope project --project ~/your-game gives each its own server in a .mcp.json in the game's folder. Without it, one server works on one project, and the install says when it kept an existing one. All the tools are in the MCP reference.
documents.s: Working with Claude Code over MCP

documents.t: You'll make a copper still: concept art, a 3D model, a game mesh, then put it in Godot. About 10 minutes on a 24 GB GPU, most of it waiting for the models.

Gen Studio is set up, and gen doctor says everything is OK. The Minimal tier (80 GB) is enough for this tutorial. You have a Godot 4 project somewhere on disk. New to the screens? Read the tour first.

A project is a folder that holds your assets, usually one per game. On Home, under Projects, press New project…. Pick a Target look (the era your game looks like, it sets the polygon budget), then an empty folder. Pick PS2 or PS3 for this one. The target look and the default profile live in gen-project.toml in that folder, and you can change them in Settings → Project.

Press All kinds… on Home (or Ctrl+N) and pick 3D prop under Props & scenery. The form shows the steps it will run. Write what you want in Prompt: a squat copper alembic still with a round belly on an iron tripod, green patina at the seams Press the sparkle beside Asset name for a name from the prompt, or type copper_still. Say what it's made of and how worn it is. The camera and the plain background are added for you. Press Generate. On the command line, from the project folder: gen make prop "a squat copper alembic still with a round belly on an iron tripod, green patina at the seams" --asset copper_still

The asset opens with one step on the rail: Concept. It draws a picture. Each try is a take. Don't like it? Press Retake; the old one stays, side by side in the strip. Click a take to see it, and Use this take to build on it. Fix it here Make two or three concept takes before you go on. Fixing a shape in the picture is quicker than fixing it in 3D.

Press Run to end in the toolbar. New steps appear on the rail as they start: Prepped cut-out cuts the picture out. Mesh builds a dense 3D model from it. Game mesh rebuilds that inside your target look's polygon budget and bakes the texture. To go one step at a time instead, press Run next in the bar above the take.

Open Game mesh, then Open large (or double-click). Drag to turn it, scroll to zoom, press 3 for the wireframe and 7 for the UV checker. The side panel shows the triangles against the budget. Not happy? Change a value in the form, or go back and use another concept take. The steps after it turn stale, and Re-run stale rebuilds them.

Press Export to Godot in the toolbar. The first time, pick your Godot project's folder. gen export copper_still ~/your-godot-game The .glb lands in res://assets/gen/copper_still/. Drag it into a scene.
A project, a target look and a profile. Steps, takes, and the take in use. Run to end, and exporting to Godot. Next: a character, from concept to Godot.
Film yourself doing a move, and put it on your character. About 5 minutes, plus filming.
A rigged character (see a character, from concept to Godot). This needs the motion-capture model: GEM-X at Balanced, SAM 3D Body at Quality. The app asks before it downloads one.

About 5 seconds, the whole body in frame, the camera still, a plain background if you can. Film side-on for walks, front-on for gestures. Fitted clothes track better than baggy ones that hide the knees. Trim the video to the move. The start and the end matter for loops.
Copy the video into your project folder. Open the character, press New clip, and type its path under Or a video file (motion capture), relative to the project.

The clip's step tracks your body and retargets it to the character's skeleton. Open the clip large: drag the timeline, or press play. A clip loops and stays in place by default: the end meets the start, and the hips don't wander. To change that, make the clip from a job file with loop: false or in_place: false.
Motion capture from a plain video. What makes a clip loop and stay in place. Next: sound for a game.
Describe a shader in a sentence and get a .gdshader that compiles in Godot, with sliders for what you want to tweak. About 2 minutes at Fast.

Press All kinds…, then Shader. Say where it goes, what it looks like and what you want to change later: a flickering green witchlight glow with a soft pulsing core and a thin bright rim; tweakable colour and pulse speed Press Generate.

Gemma writes the shader and Godot compiles it. Compile errors go back to Gemma until it compiles. Then Gemma looks at a preview and fixes what's missing: up to eight rounds at Balanced. The take keeps the best-scored round. Its notes are in the take's judge.json. Each uniform with a hint_range is a slider in Godot's inspector. Not quite right? Retake with a clearer description. Name the surface (2D sprite or 3D mesh), the colours and what moves.
Press Export to Godot, then make a ShaderMaterial on your mesh or sprite and pick the .gdshader. Set its uniforms in the inspector.
With Settings → Extensions → Who reviews a shader's look set to Claude Code, looks wait for Claude Code's verdict instead of Gemma's. See Claude Code over MCP.
Shaders written and compiled for you, with sliders. The judge rounds, and how to steer a retake. Next: a base body and an outfit.
A sound effect, a few voiced lines and a looping theme for one small scene: a herbalist's shop. About 10 minutes.

Press All kinds…, then Sound effect under Sound. Write a thick potion bubbling in an iron cauldron, slow wet pops. Say the source and the action, and keep it to one event. gen run bubble.yaml # kind: sfx, prompt: ..., seconds: 2, variants: 4 You get several variants of the same sound (a round robin), so it doesn't sound the same twice in game. Listen to each, then press Pick this one on the ones you keep. Clean up takes out noise and lifts a dull recording, and Effects opens the mixer: layers, EQ, reverb, or a VST3 plugin you own. See clean up a recording and the mixer and layers.

Press All kinds…, then Dialogue under Writing. Write what happens and name the characters: A traveller asks the herbalist for something to stop a fever; she asks where he caught it, and doesn't like the answer It writes the scene as a Dialogue Manager file for Godot, with stable keys. Add the Voice lines step after it. Give each speaker a voice: designed from a description (a warm elderly woman, unhurried), or a free AivisHub voice for Japanese. Each line is spoken, and lip-sync shapes come with it.

Press All kinds…, then Music. Name the mood, the instruments and the tempo: a gentle folk tune on harp and wooden flute, a forest village at dawn, warm and unhurried Set Length, BPM and Key, or leave them to the model. Add Stems to split it into drums, bass, vocals and the rest; add MIDI for a MIDI file of each. See stems and MIDI.
Export to Godot gives .ogg files with their loop points set, and a sound effect's variants side by side, ready for an AudioStreamRandomizer. WAV and FLAC are in Settings → Project → Sound.
Variants for sound effects, and picking them. Dialogue, voices and lines. Music with loop points, stems and MIDI. Next: a shader from a description.
Dress one body in many outfits, and swap them at runtime in Godot. About an hour at Fast for the body and four pieces; most of that is the model and rig steps.
documents.s: A base body and an outfit

documents.t: Press All kinds…, then Base body under Characters & bodies. Set Base to underwear, a plain bodysuit or a mannequin, and write a young adult man, athletic build, short dark hair. It runs a character's steps, and the concept keeps the shapes clean (bare feet, short hair) so clothes fit onto them. asset: hero kind: body base: underwear prompt: a young adult man, athletic build, short dark hair

Make each piece as a Wearable for that body, one at a time: a white linen shirt, a long leather coat, leather boots, a short wool cape. Slot and Layer are Auto. The coat is outer torso on layer 2, so it's fitted over the shirt on layer 1. Make the inner layers first: a piece is fitted over what exists when it's made. A cape gets bone chains so it swings.

Press Wardrobe on the body. Each piece shows its slot, its layer and what it was fitted over. A clash (two pieces in one slot and layer) is flagged at the top. Check the pieces you want together, name the outfit and press Save outfit. gen outfit hero travel shirt coat boots cape

Export the body and each piece. Then: const Wardrobe := preload("res://assets/gen/wardrobe.gd") Wardrobe.wear_outfit($Hero, "res://assets/gen/hero/outfits.json", "travel") Wardrobe.unequip($Hero, "back") # the cape off The body under what's worn is hidden, so it can't poke through.
A base body that clothes fit onto. Pieces in slots and layers, fitted over each other. Outfits, and swapping them in Godot. More: how wearables, fitting and cloth work.

Everything about one thing, one page each. Every page has the same shape: an at-a-glance box, how it works, how to use it, its settings, tips, troubleshooting and related pages. Asset kinds: everything you can make. Steps: every step, the model each profile runs, its fields and prompt tips. Extensions: the packs of models and steps, their weights and licences. The words are in the glossary. New here? Start with the tutorials.

The packs of models and steps, their weights and licences. Turn them on and off in Settings → Extensions. gen.ace-step Game music with ACE-Step 1.5 XL turbo on ComfyUI, then loop points and loudness in its own env. gen.aivis Japanese voices from AivisHub (AivisSpeech's Style-Bert-VITS2 models, ONNX on the CPU): a voice imported from Find free assets is pinned by its file's sha256, then speaks dialogue lines with Rhubarb lip-sync. gen.anime Anime characters and 2D art on Anima (spec 013; WAI-Anima, Anima Turbo for the fast profiles): free images, characters, shots, sprite and portrait sets, facesets, reactions and backgrounds. NoobAI-XL is an add-on (gen.anime-noobai). gen.anime-noobai NoobAI-XL for the anime pack (an add-on of gen.anime, ADR-0013): every anime step as another Model, with NoobAI's own tools: IP-Adapter references, OpenPose poses, the inpainting and canny ControlNets, DMD2 for the fast profiles and the kashimu chibi LoRA. NoobAI's official quality tags and negative. gen.audio-fx The Effects rack (spec 010): an ordered chain of Pedalboard effects, real spaces (Voxengo impulse responses) and free VST3 plugins after a sound or track, in its own CPU env. Plugins run here, never in the app. gen.audio-restore Clean up's model help (spec 010): FlashSR (one-step audio super-resolution to 48 kHz) restores a dull top end at Balanced and Quality on PS3/PS4; SonicMaster (Apache-2.0) repairs and masters a track at Quality; it's optional (the Music repair bundle) because it needs Stability AI's gated VAE. Called by the Clean up step, not steps of their own. gen.chord PBR maps from a texture image with CHORD (Ubisoft La Forge): base colour, normal, roughness, metalness. Research-only licence (recorded). gen.concept Concept art for image-to-3D: Qwen-Image 2.1 bf16 (quality), FLUX.3 klein (balanced), Z-Image-Turbo (fast) and SDXL + DMD2 (ultra fast) on ComfyUI. gen.gem-x Motion capture from video with NVIDIA GEM-X (SOMA body, contact/IK post-processing), written as a BVH. Commercial use allowed. gen.hy-motion Text to motion with Tencent HY-Motion 1.0 via hymotion-local (Qwen3-8B text encoder offloaded to RAM): BVH at 30 fps, Mixamo bone names. gen.hy3d-paint Paint texture: Hunyuan3D-Paint 2.1 paints albedo, roughness and metallic onto a model you have (or made) from one reference image; the core bakes them back onto the original mesh, keeping its topology and rig. ~21 GB of VRAM. Tencent Hunyuan non-commercial licence (no EU/UK/KR). gen.momask Text to motion with MoMask (masked residual transformer, HumanML3D): a quick BVH at 20 fps. gen.moss-sfx Sound effects with MOSS-SoundEffect v2 (1.3B DiT, 48 kHz, up to 30 s) in its own env; variants by seed. The Fast recipe; Balanced and Quality are Woosh (gen.woosh). gen.pixel Pixel art and chiptune (spec 031): sprites, characters, icons and tile sheets as true pixels from the image models you have; chiptune tracks, Chip render (a track's stems replayed on NES, Genesis, SNES or PS1 chips) and retro sound effects. No new models. gen.quaternius Text to motion without a model: the closest clip from Quaternius' CC0 Universal Animation Library, by name. gen.qwen-edit Character turnarounds: Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 + multi-angle LoRA (fast, balanced) or one Qwen-Image 2.1 four-view sheet (quality), on ComfyUI core nodes; Frame in 3D, Edit with a prompt and Relight (LightingRemap). gen.qwen-tts Character voices with Qwen3-TTS 1.7B: design a voice from a description, then speak every dialogue line in it, with Rhubarb lip-sync. gen.retopo Low-poly retopology tiers (PyMeshLab, Blender Decimate, QuadriFlow) with a bake from the kept high-poly. gen.sam3d-body Motion capture from video with Meta's SAM 3D Body on ComfyUI core nodes (SAM 3.1 tracking, MoGe field of view, smoothing, BVH). gen.sfx Sound effects with Stable Audio 3 Small-SFX on ComfyUI (Ultra fast); round-robin variants, trimmed, era effects and loudness in the core. gen.stems Stems and MIDI from music (spec 012): BS-RoFormer SW splits a track into six stems; Basic Pitch turns each into MIDI and one song.mid. gen.text Game text tools on the managed llama.cpp: JSON-schema output, pydantic-validated with retries. gen.texture Seamless tiling textures on ComfyUI (the concept models plus a native seam pass), finished by fidelity in the core: CLUT and dither for PS1/PS2, normal and roughness maps for PS3, a Godot material. gen.trellis2 Image to low-poly GLB with TRELLIS.2 on ComfyUI core nodes: BiRefNet prep, decimate to budget, bake (ADR-0008). gen.unirig Rigging: SkinTokens (UniRig's successor) makes the skeleton and skin weights in one step (rig; the character pipeline's Rig step) (UniRig was removed in spec 027). gen.woosh Sound effects with Sony AI's Woosh (48 kHz): DFlow (distilled, 4 steps) at Balanced, Flow (adaptive solver) at Quality; DVFlow gives an animated effect its sound from the clip. Weights CC-BY-NC: outputs are non-commercial too.

Everything you can make, one page each. In the app, these are in New asset. Background A scene with nobody in it, at other times of day (same layout), with optional parallax layers. Anime character Define a character once (a full-body sheet and their tags); then shoot them as often as you like. Anime image An Anima drawing with its background: any characters, framing and shape. Reactions (chibi or full size) A whole drawing per expression, cut out: lively, not lined up; for chat, menus or a desktop chibi. 2D rig (cut-out animation) A transparent shot split into parts on Godot bones: breathing, sway and a head tilt, hair that swings. Sprite or portrait set One shot in every expression, with talking and blinking, a faceset, and Ren'Py and Godot files. Shot of a character A character in any framing (full body to head), cut out, on white or in a scene. Barks Short lines for a character in idle, combat, hurt and victory; then translations. Base body A plain body (underwear, a bodysuit or a mannequin) that wardrobe pieces fit onto. Character Concept, turnaround, 3D, game mesh and a skeleton to review; then skin and clips. Retro sound effect Coins, jumps, lasers and explosions, made by a generator in a moment. Chiptune A chip-flavoured track from a description. To hear a track on real chip voices: Stems, MIDI, then add Chip render. Dialogue A scene of lines with stable keys, as a Godot Dialogue Manager file; then translations. Character model Your FBX, OBJ, GLB, VRM or .blend. A rigged humanoid gets clips straight away. Music file A track you have, at the project's loudness and era. Prop model Your own model as a prop's mesh, ready to texture, paint or export. Sound file A sound you have, finished like a made one (trim, era, loudness). Shader file A .gdshader you have, kept with its licence. Free texture Free voice Item text Name, descriptions and flavour text as checked JSON. Lore check Any text compared with your lore files: contradictions and unclear claims. Mesh from an image Your own picture of one object, turned into a low-poly model. Clip from a video Clip from a description Music A looping track at the project's loudness and sample rate. Names A list of names with meanings, in the style you describe. Pixel character A full-body character as true pixels. Pixel icon A UI or item icon, 32 px by default. Pixel sprite A prop, creature or object as true pixels with a limited palette. Pixel tiles A sheet of tiles cut at their borders, 16 or 32 px, with one palette. Prop From a prompt: concept art, a cut-out, then a low-poly model checked in Godot. Rig again Sound effect Round-robin variants of one sound, trimmed, levelled and given the target look's era. Shader A Godot shader written from your description, compiled in Godot until it works. Texture A seamless tile at the target look, with its maps and a Godot material. Effect Fire, smoke, sparks or magic: a sprite, then a flipbook animated by a video model. Voice A character's voice from a description, frozen as the reference for its lines. Wearable Armour, clothing or an accessory for a rigged character, fitted and skinned to it.

At a glance Kind body In New asset Characters & bodies → Base body Pipeline body, starting at Concept Review Rig Job file kind: body CLI gen run <job>.yaml A base body is a plain body that a wardrobe fits onto: underwear, a skin-tight bodysuit, or a smooth mannequin. It runs the character's steps, and its concept keeps the shapes clean: bare feet, short or tied-back hair, no accessories.

Pieces (wearables) made for the body are fitted onto it, each over the pieces on lower layers. Each piece records the body vertices it covers, and in Godot wardrobe.gd hides those while it's worn. Outfits are named sets of pieces: gen outfit <body> <name> <pieces…>.

At a glance Kind character In New asset Characters & bodies → 3D game character Pipeline character, starting at Concept Review Rig Job file kind: character CLI gen run <job>.yaml or gen make character "…" A character: concept art in an A-pose, four views, a 3D model, a game mesh, then a rig (skeleton and skin weights) and as many clips as you like.

The concept is worded for image-to-3D: an A-pose with the arms away from the body, open hands, hair in solid locks clear of the face. Turnaround draws the four views; Mesh builds from all four (Pixal3D multiview); Game mesh fits the budget; Rig (SkinTokens) makes the skeleton and weights in one pass, with bones named for Godot's humanoid profile. Long hair gets bone chains on the Rig step (Cloth: Auto).

Keep held things out of the concept: a sword fused to a hand can't be rigged. Make it a prop. Review the rig with the test poses before making clips: fixing a joint later means redoing the clips' retarget. A whole cast in one style: keep the same project and wording ("stylised 3D game character").

Left and right swapped in the turnaround: the step warns; retake it. A joint in the wrong place: move it in the joint editor, then retake Rig with Keep the skeleton. Fingers fused: expected at low budgets; PS3 and PS4 keep more of them.

At a glance Kind wearable In New asset Characters & bodies → Wearable Pipeline wearable, starting at Design Review Design Job file kind: wearable CLI gen run <job>.yaml A wearable is one piece of clothing, armour or an accessory, made for one rigged character or base body, fitted to its shape and skinned to its skeleton so it follows every animation.

Design redraws the character's own four renders wearing the piece (Qwen-Image-Edit) and cuts it out (SAM 3.1); the masks have to agree. Mesh builds it by one of three routes: follows the body (boots, gloves, shirts: made from the body's surface), rigid (helmets: built in 3D, then fitted), or hanging sheet (capes: the back view's outline hung behind the body with folds). Fit hugs it onto the body (and over lower layers) and pushes it out to the clearance; Paint colours it from the views; Wear copies the body's skin weights onto it, adds cloth chains for what hangs, and checks the poke in test poses and the swing in Godot.
In the app: New asset → Characters & bodies → Wearable. As a job file: asset: my_wearable kind: wearable prompt: …

One piece at a time: "leather boots", not "boots and gloves". The words choose the route and the slot: "boots" follows the body, "helmet" is rigid, "cape" hangs. Override with Route and Slot. Clearance is how far off the body it sits: raise it for thick materials and where the body pokes through.

The body pokes through at the knees or elbows: raise Clearance and run on from Fit; wear.json lists the poke per pose. A view shows the wrong piece: retake Design; the view that disagrees most is redrawn automatically once. A cape is too short: say the length ("a long cape down to the knees").

Field Type Default What it does Model model choice (WAI-Anima, NoobAI-XL) WAI-Anima Which model runs this step; an add-on extension can add more. Place prompt longtext The place in Danbooru tags: indoors, classroom, desks, window, afternoon; or outdoors, shrine, torii, forest, stone path. Nobody is drawn. Avoid negative text Tags to keep out, e.g. people, text. (advanced) Shape aspect choice (stage, wide, square) stage The picture's shape: VN stage (16:9) for scenes, Square for a portrait's background. Times of day times text evening, night The same scene again at: morning, day, evening, night, rain, snow (comma-separated; empty for none). Parallax layers parallax bool False A sky layer and a scene layer of each picture, for scrolling at different speeds.

Anima (WAI-Anima) (ultra_fast, fast, balanced, quality): A place with nobody in it, for visual novels and dialogue scenes; the same place again at other times of day keeps its layout. Structure: [no humans, scenery] (added for you) → [indoors or outdoors] → [the place] → [its objects] → [time and weather] → [light and mood]. Name the place and a few things in it: 'indoors, classroom, desks, window, chalkboard'. Time of day here is the first picture's; the Times of day field adds the others (evening, night, rain, snow) with the same layout. Wide shapes (VN stage, 16:9) suit scenery; Square is for portraits' backgrounds. Light words set the mood: 'warm lighting', 'sunbeams', 'moonlight', 'neon lights'. Parallax layers split the sky from the scene for scrolling. Avoid: People or characters: backgrounds are drawn empty so characters can go on top. Very busy prompts for small sizes: leave the model room. Examples: indoors, classroom, desks, window, chalkboard, afternoon, sunlight outdoors, shrine, torii, stone path, forest, summer, cicadas indoors, tavern, wooden tables, barrels, fireplace, warm lighting outdoors, fantasy town, market stalls, cobblestone street, day, blue sky NoobAI-XL (ultra_fast, fast, balanced, quality): A place with nobody in it, in NoobAI-XL's scenery tags; the same place at other times of day keeps its layout. Structure: [no humans, scenery] (added for you) → [indoors or outdoors] → [the place] → [its objects] → [time and weather] → [light]. Tag the place and a few things in it: 'indoors, classroom, desk, window, chalkboard'. Time of day is the first picture's; the Times of day field adds the others with the same layout. Light tags set the mood: 'sunlight', 'light rays', 'moonlight', 'neon lights'. Avoid: People: backgrounds are drawn empty. Sentences: NoobAI reads tags. Examples: indoors, classroom, desk, window, chalkboard, afternoon, sunlight outdoors, shrine, torii, stone path, forest, summer indoors, tavern, table, barrel, fireplace, warm lighting outdoors, town, market, stall, cobblestone, day, blue sky

Anima (WAI-Anima) (ultra_fast, fast, balanced, quality): The character's definition: a full-body sheet on white, front view, neutral. What you write here is the character's look; every shot of them reuses these tags (and their LoRA, once trained). Structure: [1girl / 1boy] → [species or role: elf, knight] → [hair: colour, length, style] → [eyes] → [marks: eyepatch, mole under mouth, scar] → [outfit, top to bottom] → [accessories]. Write only what's always true of the character: hair, eyes, marks, the default outfit. Poses, expressions and places belong in the Shot. List the outfit from top to bottom: 'white fur collar, burgundy vest, sleeveless, black belt, brown shorts, black gloves, brown thigh boots'. Plain tags, no weights: Anima holds a long list without them. Distinctive details (an eyepatch on one eye, a mole) are worth a word each; the LoRA learns them from the sheet. Make a few takes and use the cleanest: the sheet is what everything else copies. Avoid: Expressions and poses ('smiling, waving'): the sheet is neutral on purpose. A background: the sheet is drawn on white so it can be cut out and reused. Examples: 1girl, elf, pointy ears, very long blonde hair, black eyepatch, red eyes, mole under mouth, white fur collar, burgundy vest, sleeveless, grey turtleneck, black belt, dark brown shorts, black gloves, brown thigh boots 1boy, short messy black hair, green eyes, dark green hooded robe, brown belt, leather boots, holding a wooden staff 1girl, short silver hair, blue eyes, silver plate armor, blue cape, gauntlets, armored boots 1girl, long purple hair, yellow eyes, black witch hat, long black dress, red ribbon, brown boots NoobAI-XL (ultra_fast, fast, balanced, quality): The character's definition with NoobAI-XL: a full-body sheet on white, front view, neutral, in Danbooru tags. Every shot of the character reuses them (and their LoRA, once trained). Structure: [1girl / 1boy] → [a known character (series), if any] → [species or role] → [hair: colour, length, style] → [eyes] → [marks] → [outfit, top to bottom] → [accessories]. Danbooru tags, comma-separated, spaces not underscores: 'long hair, blonde hair, red eyes, eyepatch'. Only what's always true of the character; poses and expressions belong in the Shot. List the outfit top to bottom, one tag per garment: 'fur-trimmed collar, sleeveless jacket, turtleneck, belt, shorts, gloves, thigh boots'. NoobAI knows characters by their Danbooru names: 'frieren, sousou no frieren'. Weights are rarely needed; (tag:1.2) pushes one that keeps getting lost. Avoid: Sentences: NoobAI reads tags. Expressions, poses or a background: the sheet is neutral and on white. Quality tags (masterpiece, best quality): already added. Examples: 1girl, elf, pointy ears, very long hair, blonde hair, eyepatch, red eyes, mole under mouth, fur collar, sleeveless jacket, turtleneck, belt, shorts, gloves, thigh boots 1boy, short hair, messy hair, black hair, green eyes, hooded robe, green robe, belt, boots, staff 1girl, short hair, silver hair, blue eyes, armor, plate armor, blue cape, gauntlets, armored boots 1girl, long hair, purple hair, yellow eyes, witch hat, black dress, long dress, red ribbon, brown boots

Anima (WAI-Anima) (ultra_fast, fast, balanced, quality): A 2B anime model (Cosmos-Predict2 with a Qwen3 text encoder) trained on Danbooru. It reads Danbooru tags, plain sentences, or both mixed, and follows them much more closely than SDXL models: several characters, their outfits, who does what to whom. Structure: [how many: 1girl / 2girls / 1boy, 1girl] → [a known character and series] → [@artist] → [hair, eyes, outfit] → [expression, pose, action] → [framing: upper body, full body, cowboy shot] → [place, time, light]. Or two or more sentences saying the same. Tags are lowercase with spaces, not underscores: 'long hair, blue eyes, school uniform, smile'. Sentences work too, and mixing is fine: tags for the look, a sentence for what happens ('she laughs and points at the boy, who looks embarrassed'). Two characters: describe each one fully (hair, eyes, outfit), then what they do together. Names alone confuse it. An artist's style: '@name' (the @ matters; without it the effect is very weak). Weights need to be stronger than on SDXL models: (chibi:2) rather than (chibi:1.2). A very short prompt lets the model fill in a lot, sometimes more than you want; add detail, or 'safe' / 'nsfw' to say which. Ultra fast and Fast (Anima Turbo, 10 steps) are for trying ideas in seconds; Balanced and Quality use CFG, so Avoid works there. Quality adds a 1.5× Hires pass with the anime upscaler. Avoid: Quality tags yourself (masterpiece, best quality): they're already added. SDXL habits like piling up (tag:1.1) weights: they barely move Anima. Contradicting framing tags (portrait with full body). Examples: 1girl, solo, long silver hair, red eyes, black coat, gloves, serious, upper body, snowy forest, night, moonlight 1boy, solo, messy brown hair, green eyes, adventurer, leather armor, sword on back, smile, cowboy shot, fantasy town, market, day 2girls. the first girl has short pink hair in twintails and a frilled magical girl dress; the second has long black hair and a school uniform. they hold hands and laugh, full body, cherry blossoms, spring 1girl, solo, glasses, office lady, white shirt, pencil skirt, sitting at a desk with a computer, indoors, evening, window, city lights NoobAI-XL (ultra_fast, fast, balanced, quality): NoobAI-XL, the Model choice from the add-on: an Illustrious-based SDXL anime model trained on Danbooru and e621 tags. It follows comma-separated tags far better than sentences, knows thousands of characters, artists and outfits by their Danbooru names, and draws full scenes with backgrounds. Structure: [how many: 1girl, solo / 2boys] → [who: a known character (series)] → [hair, eyes, body] → [outfit] → [expression and pose] → [framing: upper body, full body, cowboy shot, portrait] → [place and time: classroom, sunset, rain] → [light and style: dramatic lighting, watercolor]. Use Danbooru tags, comma-separated: 'long hair, blue eyes, school uniform, smile'. Spaces, not underscores. Say how many people first: '1girl, solo', '1boy, 1girl', '2girls'. It decides the composition. Framing is a tag: 'portrait', 'upper body', 'cowboy shot' (thighs up), 'full body', 'from above', 'from side'. Known characters work by name and series: 'hatsune miku, vocaloid', 'frieren, sousou no frieren'. An artist's look comes from 'artist name' tags; use them sparingly, one or two. Weight a tag with (tag:1.2) to push it, (tag:0.8) to soften it. Backgrounds: describe the place in tags: 'indoors, classroom, window, sunlight, desk'. 'simple background, white background' for a plain one. Fast and Ultra fast (DMD2) are for trying ideas in seconds; Balanced and Quality use CFG, so Avoid works there and the drawing is cleaner. Quality adds a 1.5× Hires pass for detail. Avoid: Long sentences: NoobAI reads tags; a sentence becomes a jumble of half-matched tags. Quality tags yourself (masterpiece, best quality): they're already added. Contradicting framing tags (portrait with full body). Examples: 1girl, solo, long silver hair, red eyes, black coat, gloves, serious, upper body, snowy forest, night, moonlight 1boy, solo, messy brown hair, green eyes, adventurer, leather armor, sword on back, smile, cowboy shot, fantasy town, market, daytime 1girl, solo, short pink hair, twintails, magical girl, frilled dress, wand, winking, full body, starry sky, sparkles 2girls, school uniform, holding hands, walking, from behind, cherry blossoms, school, spring, petals

At a glance Step id anime_rig2d Used by anime_rig2d Runs fast: SAM 3.1 parts Time 40–40 s VRAM 10 GB Extension gen.anime CLI gen retake <asset> anime_rig2d --set <field>=<value> Claude Code fields, retake, look, use A 2D cut-out rig of a transparent shot: parts on Godot bones (Skeleton2D and Polygon2D, no third-party runtime) with idle, sway and head-tilt animations.

SAM 3.1 finds the hair, face, arms, hands, sleeves and legs (each pair by looking twice); the torso is the rest. Limbs split at their middle; hair below the chin is back hair. Joints come from the parts' shapes. Each part's hidden area is filled in smoothly so moving a limb shows no hole (checked at 15°). Every part gets a grid mesh weighted to its bones. Godot plays each animation in the check; rig.json records the parts, bones and holes, and found.png shows what SAM found.

Two models (the Model choice): FlowEdit (WAI-Anima), the default: the picture is redrawn from its own prompt towards the same prompt plus rim-light words, with the character's LoRA and the rim light LoRA, so the line art and colours stay and only the lit edges change. Intensity 1 is a crisp, thin rim; 5 is wide and bright (the most before colours elsewhere start to shift). Seed 0 redraws with the picture's own noise. A transparent shot is cut out again by ViTMatte around its own outline, so the lit edges stay sharp. Qwen-Image-Edit 2511: Qwen relights only inside a band along the edges facing the light, never the face; Strength sets how deep, and "Keep only the rim colour" drops anything else it painted. Cut-out (advanced): ViTMatte (sharp edges, keeps the line art) or ToonOut only (the shot's alpha as it was).

At a glance Step id anime_shot Used by anime_shot Runs ultra fast: Anima Turbo, 10 steps (WAI-Anima) fast: Anima Turbo, 10 steps (WAI-Anima) balanced: WAI-Anima, 30 steps (WAI-Anima) quality: WAI-Anima, 36 steps (WAI-Anima) ultra fast: NoobAI-XL + DMD2, 8 steps + IP-Adapter, ToonOut (NoobAI-XL) fast: NoobAI-XL + DMD2, 8 steps + IP-Adapter, ToonOut (NoobAI-XL) balanced: NoobAI-XL, 25 steps + IP-Adapter, ToonOut (NoobAI-XL) quality: NoobAI-XL, 30 steps + IP-Adapter, ToonOut (NoobAI-XL) Time 6–25 s VRAM 10 GB Extension gen.anime, gen.anime-noobai CLI gen retake <asset> anime_shot --set <field>=<value> Claude Code fields, retake, look, use One shot of a defined anime character (or up to four): framing, pose, background and expression, drawn by Anima with the character's tags and LoRA.

The character's sheet tags (and LoRA, once trained) lead the prompt; the Framing, Pose and Background choices add theirs; your Shot text says the rest. A transparent shot is cut out by ToonOut, then ViTMatte redraws the edge so thin outlines on hair tips and fingers stay (advanced Cut-out: ToonOut only gives the older, softer edge). Close framings are drawn waist-up and cropped around the face, then given a detail pass. At Balanced and Quality the shot is finished: an AnimeSharp upscale to 1.5×, a light refine, and a face pass. With three or more characters each is redrawn in its own place (Layout) and the faces are counted, one per place.

Field Type Default What it does Prompt prompt longtext One subject, plainly described; the app adds the framing and background Enhance the prompt enhance bool False Gemma 4 rewrites the prompt in detail first (the rewrite is saved with the take) Control image control file Optional: a sketch, photo or render whose outline the concept follows (Fast) (advanced)

Say materials, colours and shapes; leave out camera and lighting words (they're added). Restyle (on a take) redraws it from the old one with a new description: the shape stays. Vary region redraws one part ("the helmet"). Z-Image-Turbo / FLUX.3 klein: props (fast, balanced): Alibaba's 6B few-step image model for one game object that becomes a 3D model. It reads plain sentences well and follows long, concrete descriptions; it has no negative prompt. Structure: [what it is] → [silhouette and proportions] → [parts and how they join] → [materials and finish] → [colours and wear] → [style]. Start with the silhouette: 'a squat barrel, wider in the middle', 'a tall narrow lantern'. The 3D steps rebuild the outline first. List the parts and how they connect: 'iron hoops nailed around oak staves', 'a ring handle riveted to the lid'. Name materials precisely: 'tarnished brass', 'split dark oak', 'chipped red enamel'. Wear makes it a game asset: 'scratched edges', 'rust in the seams', 'faded paint'. One object only. Things sitting on it (a candle on the chest) become part of the mesh. Avoid thin floating parts (chains, ropes, loose straps): image-to-3D merges or drops them. Say what you want instead of what you don't: there is no negative prompt. Style words set the era: 'low-poly PS1 game asset', 'hand-painted fantasy prop', 'clean 3D render'. Avoid: Scenes, rooms or several objects: the steps after concept want one subject alone. Camera, lighting and background words: they fight the framing the app adds. Text or logos on the object. Examples: A wooden treasure chest with a domed lid, iron bands and corner caps, a brass lock plate, scratched dark oak, low-poly PS1 game asset style A squat oak barrel, wider in the middle, three iron hoops, a wooden tap near the base, water-stained staves A ship's oil lantern: blackened iron frame, four cracked amber glass panes, a ring handle on top, hand-painted fantasy style A short sword with a leather-wrapped grip, a bronze cross-guard shaped like wings, a slightly nicked blade, clean 3D render Qwen-Image 2.1: props (quality): Alibaba's 20B image model (bf16 here) with a Qwen3-VL text encoder: the most faithful to long, precise descriptions, counts and materials; best when the subject must match exactly. Field Type Default What it does The scene prompt longtext Who talks, where, what happens and how it ends; the lore folder is passed along Characters characters text Comma-separated speaker names, as they appear in the game Lines length int 2.0…40.0 10 About how many lines the dialogue has.

Gemma 4 (26B A4B and E4B) (fast, ultra_fast): Writes one dialogue scene as checked JSON (speaker, emotion and text per line, each with a stable [ID:KEY]), rendered as a Godot Dialogue Manager file. The lore folder is passed along. Structure: [who is talking] + [where and when] + [what each wants] + [what happens] + [how it ends]. Put the speaker names in the Characters field. Say what each character wants: scenes with a goal and an obstacle read better than chat. Give the ending: 'she leaves with the key', 'he refuses and walks off'. Name the tone: dry, warm, menacing, comic. Keep scenes short (6-14 lines); write several scenes rather than one long one. Facts the scene must use belong in lore/*.md, where every text tool sees them. Line keys stay stable when you retake: voice, lip-sync and translations only redo lines whose text changed. Avoid: Branching choices: this tool writes one linear scene; split branches into separate scenes. Stage directions inside the text: emotions have their own field. More than six speakers in one scene. Examples: Mara arrives at the harbour at night and asks the old keeper why the lighthouse is dark; he admits he stopped lighting it after the Drowned Bell rang, and gives her the key A blacksmith haggles with a broke young knight over a sword repair; she agrees to fix it if he clears the rats from her cellar Two guards at a gate argue about whether ghosts are real until something knocks from the outside The innkeeper warns a traveller not to go up the hill after dark; the traveller laughs and goes anyway

Field Type Default What it does Style prompt longtext Comma-separated tags: genre, mood, instruments, tempo feel Length (seconds) duration float 5.0…240.0 60 How long the track is; a loop's length is matched to whole bars. BPM bpm int 40.0…240.0 100 Beats per minute; empty lets the model choose. Key keyscale text A minor The key, e.g. C major or A minor; empty lets the model choose. (advanced) Time signature timesignature choice (3, 4, 6) 4 Beats per bar: 4/4 for most game music, 3/4 for a waltz. (advanced) Lyrics lyrics longtext Section tags on their own lines ([verse], [chorus]); empty makes an instrumental (advanced) Seamless loop loop bool True Find a loop point and cut the track to it Era reverb reverb choice (default, on, off) default PS1 and PS2 add their console-style reverb by default; PS3 and PS4 leave it off (advanced)

Name the mood, instruments and tempo: "a calm village theme, acoustic guitar and flute, 90 bpm, loops". Length, BPM, Key and Time signature pin what the model would otherwise choose. Stems and MIDI come after, as manual steps. ACE-Step 1.5 (ultra_fast, fast): An open music model that takes two inputs: a caption of tags for the sound, and lyrics with section tags for the structure. Gen Studio makes instrumental loops by default. Structure: Comma-separated tags: [genre], [mood], [lead instruments], [rhythm and tempo feel], [production or era], [use]. Example: 'orchestral, heroic, brass and strings, steady march rhythm, cinematic, video game overworld'. Tags do the heavy lifting: be specific about genre, instruments and mood. Combine a few style tags for a more particular sound: 'chiptune, 8-bit, upbeat, arpeggios'. Name the instruments you want to hear: 'accordion', 'pizzicato strings', 'taiko drums', 'analog synth pad'. Describe the game use too: 'shop music', 'boss battle', 'calm village', 'dungeon ambience'. For instrumental music, keep lyrics as [Instrumental] (the default) and you can add 'instrumental, no vocals' to the tags. Set BPM and key in the fields rather than in the prompt; they are passed to the model directly. Loops: keep the style steady (no 'builds to a climax'): the loop finder needs matching start and end sections. If you add lyrics, use section tags on their own lines ([verse], [chorus], [bridge], [outro]) and 6-10 syllables per line. Avoid: Song or artist names: describe the sound instead. Long sentences about a story: the caption is about sound, not plot. Contradicting tags ('calm, aggressive'). Examples: calm harbour town, acoustic guitar, accordion, soft hand percussion, warm, folk, gentle sway, village theme heroic orchestral overworld, brass fanfare, strings, snare march, adventurous, cinematic, video game dark dungeon ambience, low drones, sparse piano, distant metallic hits, tense, slow, atmospheric chiptune, 8-bit, upbeat, fast arpeggios, square wave lead, retro platformer level ACE-Step 1.5 (lyrics) (ultra_fast, fast): ACE-Step sings the lyrics in the Style prompt's voice and genre; section tags set the song's structure. Empty makes an instrumental. Structure: Section tags on their own lines ([verse], [chorus], [bridge], [outro]), each followed by short lines of 6-10 syllables. Put each section tag on its own line: [intro], [verse], [chorus], [bridge], [outro]. Keep lines short, 6-10 syllables, and rhyme them in pairs. Repeat the chorus word for word: it makes the song's hook. Add a voice to the Style prompt (female vocals, male choir) to choose who sings. [Instrumental] alone makes a track without vocals. Avoid: Long lines: they get rushed or cut. Stage directions in the lyrics (sing softly): put the feel in the Style prompt. Lyrics on a loop: the loop finder needs matching sections, a song rarely has them. Examples: [verse] Lanterns burning by the shore Waiting for the ships once more [chorus] Raise the sails and sing along The sea will carry us home [verse] Iron gates and silent halls Shadows dancing on the walls [chorus] Hold the line, hold the light [verse] Snow is falling on the town Every roof in white and brown [chorus] Stay a while, stay a while

Z-Image-Turbo (pixel sprite) (ultra_fast, fast): The best of the installed models for pixel art: chunky, clean, readable sprites. Pixelate then turns the drawing into true pixels. Structure: [size and kind of subject], [one or two things it holds or wears], [main colours]. Example: 'a small knight with a sword and shield, silver armour, red plume'. One subject. Pixel art reads by silhouette: say what makes the shape. Name one or two strong colours: they become the palette's accents. A small, simple subject survives the shrink better than a detailed one. Details under a pixel or two vanish at 48 px: a belt buckle may, a sword won't. A new size or palette is a retake of Pixelate only, with no GPU; retake the drawing when the shape is wrong. Avoid: 'Four frames in a row' or 'sprite sheet': every model draws near-identical poses. Animation is not in this version. Backgrounds and scenes: Pixelate cuts around one subject on a flat background. Style words like 'pixel art', '16-bit' or 'white background': they are added for you. Examples: a small knight with a sword and shield, silver armour, red plume a green slime monster with big round eyes a wooden treasure chest with gold bands a red mushroom with white spots FLUX.3 klein (pixel sprite) (balanced): Draws convincing pixel art with finer shading, smaller in the frame; Pixelate crops to it. At 32 px its shading merges: stay at 48 or 64. Structure: [size and kind of subject], [what it holds or wears], [main colours]. Keep Pixelate at 48 px or more: its shading is finer than Z-Image's. Ask for clear colour blocks: 'silver armour, red plume' rather than textures. Avoid: Style words like 'pixel art' or 'white background': they are added for you. Examples: a small knight with a sword and shield, dark cloak, gold cross a red health potion bottle with a cork a little robot with a round head and antenna a brown bear standing Qwen-Image 2.1 (pixel sprite) (quality): The most faithful to a long description; its hatched shading can turn into busy pixels. Slower, and not better at pixel art than Z-Image. Structure: [subject], [details], [main colours]. Use it when a specific detail or combination matters: a blue tabard with a white star. Avoid: Style words: they are added for you. Textures and hatching: they become noise. Examples: a small knight with a sword and shield, silver armour, a blue tabard with a white star a chef with a tall hat holding a frying pan a mechanical owl with brass feathers a fox archer in a green hood

Field Type Default What it does Model model choice (, WAI-Anima, Z-Image, Qwen-Image-Edit 2511, NoobAI-XL) Same as the picture: the model that drew it redraws the area (Z-Image for any other); Qwen-Image-Edit changes it by prompt. Area mask mask Draw the area to repaint (brush, lasso, box, or click with SAM 3.1). Nothing outside it changes. Strength strength float 0.05…1.0 0.5 How much the area may change: about 0.3-0.5 keeps its shape and colour (fixes, sketched colour), 0.5-0.7 reinterprets it, 1.0 draws it anew from what is around it. Prompt prompt longtext What the picture shows; filled in from the picture's own prompt. Say what the area should be if it should change. Find by name find text Or name the part ('the left hand', 'the helmet'): SAM 3.1 finds it and adds it to the area. Preset preset choice (none, hands, face) none Fix hands and Fix face find each hand or the face (SAM 3.1) and redraw each up close, at 0.5 and 0.4; the Area is not needed. Grow (px) grow int 0.0…64.0 8 How far past what you drew the repaint reaches. (advanced) Soft edge (px) blend int 0.0…64.0 16 How wide the edge that fades into the picture is (narrower at a low Strength). (advanced) Context context float 1.0…4.0 1.5 How much of the picture around the area the model sees, as a multiple of its size (at least 512 px); the crop is redrawn at 1024. (advanced) Match colour match_colour bool True Shifts the repaint's colours to the picture's, measured just around the area, so no patch shows. (advanced) The change change longtext What to do to the area, as an instruction: 'make the cape red', 'fix the left hand', 'remove the logo'.

Retouch: Redraw (Anima + Anima-LLLite inpaint) (ultra_fast, fast, balanced, quality): Repaints only the area you mark with the picture's own Anima model and the character's LoRA. The prompt is the picture's own tags, filled in for you. Structure: The picture's tags, then tags for the area: 'detailed hands, five fingers', 'open mouth, smile', 'red ribbon'. Quality tags are added for you. Low Strength (0.3-0.5) fixes detail in the same drawing; 0.6-0.8 redraws the part; 1.0 draws it anew from around it. Fix hands and Fix face find each hand or the face and redraw it up close: no drawing needed. Add the tag for the change at the end ('red ribbon', 'closed eyes'); keep the character's tags. Avoid: Natural-language sentences: Anima reads Danbooru tags best. Removing the character's own tags. Examples: 1girl, silver hair, detailed hands, five fingers 1girl, smile, open mouth, detailed face 1girl, closed eyes 1girl, red ribbon, hair ribbon Retouch: Redraw (Z-Image) (ultra_fast, fast, balanced, quality): Repaints only the area you mark. The prompt is the picture's own, filled in for you: keep it, and add what the area should be if it should change. Structure: The picture's prompt, then what the area should show: the subject, then the part in a few words ('… , her left hand open, five fingers'). Low Strength (0.3-0.5) keeps the shape and colour and fixes detail; 0.5-0.7 reinterprets; 1.0 draws it anew. To steer a colour or shape, paint a rough blob first (Edit in Krita) and redraw at about 0.4. Mark a little past the part: Grow and Soft edge blend it in, and nothing outside the mark changes. Not the result you wanted? Reroll for another seed, or Build on this take. Avoid: Describing a different picture: the area must still fit what is around it. Big areas at 1.0: make a new take instead. Structure: One instruction, verb first: what to do to the marked part ('make …', 'replace … with …', 'remove …', 'fix …'). Name the part as it is in the picture: 'the cape', 'the left glove', 'the sign'. One change at a time; Build on the take for the next one. Mark a little past the part, so the edge of the change blends in. Avoid: Long descriptions of the whole picture: say only the change. Changes reaching past the marked area: they are cut off at its edge. Fix hands and Fix face find each hand or the face and redraw it up close: no drawing needed. Add the tag for the change at the end ('red ribbon', 'closed eyes'); keep the character's tags. Avoid: Natural-language sentences: NoobAI reads Danbooru tags best. Removing the character's own tags.
