Field Type Default What it does Sound prompt longtext Source, action, then the recording: 'a heavy wooden door creaks open slowly, close-up, dry room' Length (seconds) seconds float 0.5…30.0 2.0 How long the sound is. Variants variants int 1.0…8.0 4 Round-robin takes of the same sound, each nudged a little in pitch and level Era reverb reverb choice (default, on, off) default A room sound in the style of the project's era. (advanced)

Describe the source and the action: "a thick potion bubbling in an iron cauldron, slow wet pops". Keep it to one event; layers come in the Effects step. PS1 and PS2 roll off the top and lower the sample rate on purpose. MOSS-SoundEffect v2 (fast): OpenMOSS's 1.3B flow-matching model at 48 kHz: environments, creatures, human actions and short percussive sounds, up to 30 s. It reads full natural sentences. Structure: One plain sentence: [what makes the sound] [doing what] [where, how close], plus any detail of timing ('twice', 'then fades'). Write a natural sentence: 'A large dog barks twice in an empty courtyard.' Timing words work: 'twice', 'slowly', 'then silence', 'building up'. Name the place for the acoustics: 'in a stone cellar', 'in an open field'. Creatures and ambiences are this model's strength; it also handles human actions. It makes up to 30 s: use Fast for long ambiences (Woosh, at Balanced and Quality, makes up to 5 s). English or Chinese prompts both work. Avoid: Music, singing or speech. Lists of tags: this model was trained on captions. Examples: A large dog barks twice in an empty stone courtyard. A wooden door slams shut in a small room. A crowd of goblins chatters and cackles in a cave. Waves crash on rocks at night, with wind. Stable Audio 3 Small-SFX (ultra_fast): Stability AI's small sound-effects model, distilled to 8 steps: very fast one-shots and short loops. It follows short, concrete descriptions. Structure: [source], [action], [material or size], [recording: close or distant, dry or roomy]. A category word first helps: 'Footstep:', 'Impact:', 'UI:'. Name the source and the action: 'a sword is drawn from a leather scabbard'. Give material and size: 'small glass bottle', 'heavy iron gate'. Say how it was recorded: 'close-up, dry' for game one-shots; 'distant, echoing' for ambience. Keep the length short for one-shots (0.5–3 s); use 10–30 s for ambience loops. Ask for one event: 'a single footstep' beats 'footsteps' when you want one-shots. Use Variants for round robin: the same sound several times, slightly different each time. Avoid: Music or melodies: use the Music asset. Speech or words: use Voice. Several unrelated events in one prompt. Examples: Footstep: a single boot step on wet stone, close-up, dry Impact: a wooden sword hits a wooden shield, close-up UI: a soft, bright menu click, short A small glass potion bottle is uncorked with a pop Woosh (balanced, quality): Sony AI's sound-effect foundation model at 48 kHz, up to 5 s: DFlow (distilled, a few steps) at Balanced, Flow (adaptive solver, the best quality) at Quality. Trained on sound-effect libraries, so it reads short captions. Its licence is non-commercial, and that covers what it makes. Structure: A short caption: [the source] [the action] [a quality or place], e.g. 'sportscar engine revving and driving away quickly'. Short captions work best: 'heavy wooden door creaking open slowly'. Name the material and the action: 'glass bottle shattering on concrete'. Add how it moves or ends: 'whoosh passing left to right', 'impact with a long tail'. Keep it to one event: Woosh makes up to 5 s. Make a Fast take (MOSS) too and use Compare to pick between them. Avoid: Music, singing or speech. More than 5 s: use Fast (MOSS, up to 30 s) for long ambiences. Commercial releases: Woosh's outputs are CC-BY-NC. Examples: sportscar engine revving and driving away quickly heavy wooden door creaking open slowly sword whoosh, fast swing glass bottle shattering on concrete

Say where it's used (a 2D sprite, a 3D mesh, the sky) and what moves. Name the parameters you want to tweak ("with a uniform for the edge colour"). Shader writer (Gemma 4 + Godot compile loop) (quality, balanced, fast, ultra_fast): A general text model (Gemma 4 31B at Balanced and Quality) writes Godot 4 shading language from your description; Godot compiles it and the errors go back until it compiles. Structure: [where it goes: a 3D surface, a 2D sprite or UI, a sky] → [what it looks like] → [how it moves] → [what should be tweakable]. Say the target first: '3D surface', 'a 2D sprite effect', 'a sky'. It sets shader_type. Describe the look in shapes and colours: 'dark crust with thin glowing orange cracks'. Say how it moves: 'pulses every two seconds', 'scrolls left slowly', 'flickers'. Name the knobs you want: 'tweakable glow colour and crack width' become uniforms. Keep one effect per shader; combine them in Godot with next_pass or several materials. Field Type Default What it does Describe the motion prompt longtext One person, the body's movement, in order Length (seconds) duration float 1.0…10.0 3 How long the clip is. Frame rate fps choice (15, 30, source) Source keeps the motion's own rate Keys stepped bool Stepped keys hold each pose (the PS1 look) Static pose pose bool False One held pose instead of a motion (describe the pose): for Frame in 3D, or a pose for your game

One action per clip: "a confident walk cycle", "a two-handed sword swing". Clips loop and stay in place by default. A job file can set loop: false and in_place: false; the app's form has neither yet. HY-Motion 1.0 (balanced, quality): Tencent's billion-parameter motion model (Lite on Balanced, full on Quality). It turns an English description of one person's movement into a clip; Balanced keeps clips under 5 seconds. Structure: 'A person' + the body action + how + simple steps in order: 'A person walks forward confidently, turns left, and keeps walking with arms swinging.' Write in English and keep it under 60 words (under 30 on Balanced). Describe one person and the body's movement, in the order it happens. Add manner words: slowly, cautiously, limping, energetic, tired. Name the limbs when it matters: 'swings a sword overhead with both hands'. For a game loop (walk, idle, run), describe one steady action without a start or end pose. Short, single-action clips retarget and loop best; chain actions only when you need them. Avoid: Props and scenery the motion can't show (the model makes body movement only). Several people or interactions with another character. Camera directions. Examples: A person walks forward at a steady pace with arms swinging naturally. A person stands idle, breathing and shifting weight from one foot to the other. A person jogs forward with a relaxed, even stride. A person swings a sword overhead with both hands and strikes down. MoMask (fast): A masked-transformer motion model trained on HumanML3D. It knows everyday motions described in short, plain sentences. Structure: HumanML3D style: 'A person' / 'Someone' + one action + an optional detail: 'A person walks in a clockwise circle and stops where he began.' Start with 'A person' or 'Someone', as the training captions do. One plain sentence, one or two actions. Everyday motions work best: walking, running, jumping, sitting, waving, kicking, dancing. Add direction and counts when they matter: 'takes four steps backwards', 'turns around'. Name the side: 'kicks with the right leg', 'raises the left arm'. Avoid: Rare or acrobatic moves the dataset barely covers (it may fall back to walking). Long multi-step stories. Objects and scenery. Examples: A person is walking slowly. A person jogs forward. A person stands still and looks around. Someone is doing jumping jacks. Quaternius animation library (ultra_fast): Not a generator: it picks the best-matching clip from Quaternius' Universal Animation Library (46 hand-made, CC0 animations) by the words in your prompt. Structure: A few keywords naming the action: 'walk', 'jog forward', 'idle', 'punch', 'death', 'sitting', 'dance', 'crouch', 'roll', 'jump'. Use the action word: walk, jog or run, idle, jump, punch, shoot, roll, crouch, dance, sit, death, pick up, talk. Add 'forward' to prefer a forward-moving clip. Words like walking, runs and dies are understood (they map to walk, jog and death). A prompt with no matching word gets the idle loop. Clips ending in Loop are preferred on ties, which suits game cycles. Avoid: Descriptions of style or emotion: only action words count. Anything not in the library (climbing a ladder, swimming): pick Fast or Balanced for those. Examples: walk jog forward idle jump

Z-Image-Turbo (fast): Alibaba's 6B few-step image model. Rich, photographic surfaces; describe the material in plain sentences. No negative prompt. Structure: [material], [its parts or pattern], [colours], [wear and age], [style]. One or two plain sentences. Describe a surface, not an object: 'mossy cobblestones', not 'a cobblestone street'. Name the pattern's scale: 'small square tiles', 'large irregular flagstones', 'fine wood grain'. Even, repeating detail tiles best; one big feature (a crack across the middle) repeats visibly. Say the wear: 'chipped paint', 'rust streaks', 'polished by feet'. A style word sets the era: 'hand-painted', 'photo-sourced', 'pixel-art-like PS1 texture'. For PS1 and PS2 the app reduces the colours afterwards; strong, simple colour areas survive that best. Retake with the dice before rewriting: seams and layout vary a lot between seeds. Avoid: Perspective words (a corridor, a horizon, 'looking down the road'): textures are flat and straight-on. Lighting directions or cast shadows: baked-in light breaks when the texture is lit in the game. Single centred objects: they repeat as a grid of copies. Examples: Old cobblestones of uneven grey granite, moss in the gaps, worn smooth, photo-sourced game texture Weathered wooden planks running horizontally, dark knots, faded green paint flaking off Rusted iron plate with rivets in a regular grid, orange rust streaks over dark steel Red clay roof tiles in overlapping rows, a few chipped, sun-faded SDXL + DMD2 (4 steps) (ultra_fast): Stable Diffusion XL distilled to 4 steps. Very fast, and SDXL makes the most regular, tile-friendly surfaces. It runs at CFG 1, so the negative prompt barely matters. Structure: Short comma-separated phrases, material first: [material], [pattern], [colours], [wear], [style], 'texture'. Put the material first and end with 'texture' or 'seamless texture'. Short phrases, not sentences: CLIP reads about 75 tokens. Regular patterns (bricks, tiles, planks, weave) come out best. Colour and wear words work well: 'mossy', 'rusty', 'faded blue', 'polished'. The app adds the flat, even, straight-on framing; leave camera words out. Avoid: Text, signs or lettering: SDXL draws garbled letters. Scenes and objects: a texture is a surface. Examples: grey cobblestones, moss between stones, worn, game texture wooden planks, horizontal, dark knots, flaking green paint, texture rusty iron plate, rivet grid, orange rust streaks, texture red clay roof tiles, overlapping rows, sun-faded, texture

Keep the camera out of it: the app already asks for a static camera on black. Retake with the dice: motion varies a lot between seeds. Examples: bursts outward fast, sparks fly, then the fire curls up and fades to thin smoke the smoke puff expands slowly and thins out until it disappears the magic ring spins and pulses steadily the lightning ball crackles, arcs flicker around it Wan 2.2 I2V 14B (animated effect, Model: Wan 2.2 14B) (quality, balanced, fast): The bigger image-to-video model, two experts (one lays out the motion, one the detail), at 16 fps. With the Lightning LoRAs (Fast, Balanced) it takes about as long as the 5B and follows the motion more closely; Quality runs 20 full steps. Structure: How it moves, in order: [start] → [middle] → [end]. One or two plain sentences. It follows the order of events well: say how it starts, changes and ends. Say how it ends (fades, scatters, burns down): the 14B keeps going to that end instead of cutting. Lightning (Fast, Balanced) keeps motion a little calmer; Quality moves more but takes several minutes. For a loop, tick Loop and describe a steady motion: 'flickers and swirls steadily'. Retake with the dice: seeds still vary. Avoid: Camera moves, zooms or cuts. New objects appearing. Long stories: it's 5 seconds at most. Examples: bursts outward, then breaks into sparks that fade bursts outward fast, sparks fly, then the fire curls up and fades to thin smoke the smoke puff expands slowly and thins out until it disappears the magic ring spins and pulses steadily

Field Type Default What it does What it sounds like sound_prompt longtext Optional: words to steer it ('a fiery whoosh, crackling embers'); empty uses the effect's own prompt Variants variants int 1.0…8.0 3 How many versions of the sound to make (a round robin). (advanced)

Woosh video-to-audio (effect sound) (ultra_fast): Woosh's video-to-audio model (DVFlow, 8 s) hears the animated effect's frames and times the sound to them; these words only steer what it sounds like. Empty: the effect's own prompt is used. Structure: A short caption of the sound, not the picture: [the source or material] [the action] [a quality], e.g. 'a fiery whoosh, crackling embers'. Describe what you hear, not what you see: 'electric crackle and hum', not 'blue lightning'. Name the material: fire, ice, water, stone, metal, energy. Say how it starts and ends: 'a sharp burst, then a hissing tail'. Leave timing to the frames: the model follows the effect's motion. Keep it short: a few words beat a sentence. Avoid: Music, singing or speech. Visual words (colours, shapes, glow): they don't make a sound. Several unrelated sounds: one effect, one sound. Examples: a fiery whoosh, crackling embers electric crackle and buzzing hum icy shatter with a glassy tinkle deep magical boom, rumbling tail

Field Type Default What it does The voice prompt longtext 40-80 words: age, gender, pitch, accent, pace, texture, mood and how they speak Sample line sample longtext What the reference clip says (a varied sentence clones best); empty uses a stock line (advanced) Language language choice (English, Japanese, Chinese, Korean, German, French, Russian, Portuguese, Spanish, Italian) English The language the voice speaks.

Qwen3-TTS VoiceDesign (ultra_fast, fast): Qwen's 1.7B voice designer: it speaks the sample line in a voice made from your description, and that clip becomes the character's frozen voice for every dialogue line. 40 to 80 words work best. Structure: Who they are (age, gender, role), then the voice itself: pitch, texture (gravelly, breathy, clear), accent, pace and rhythm, then the mood and how they talk to people. Write 40-80 words: shorter descriptions give generic voices, much longer ones get ignored. Give an age and a gender first: 'A woman in her sixties', 'a boy of about twelve'. Name the texture: gravelly, husky, breathy, nasal, bright, warm, thin, booming. Pitch and pace are separate: 'low-pitched and slow', 'high and quick'. An accent works as a broad region: 'a soft Irish accent', 'a crisp upper-class English accent'. Say how they talk to people: 'patient, as if explaining to a child', 'clipped, giving orders'. One mood, not three: the voice is frozen, so a range of emotions blurs it. The Language field sets the language; describe the voice in English either way. Avoid: Real people's names ('sounds like a famous actor'): describe the voice instead. What the character says or their backstory: only how they sound matters here. Effects (robotic, echo, radio): the era effects come later in the chain. Contradictions ('deep, high-pitched voice'). Examples: An old lighthouse keeper in his seventies, deep and gravelly baritone, slow and deliberate, a soft coastal accent, tired but kind, every sentence trailing off a little as if he is half lost in memories, speaking quietly to someone he trusts. A young woman of about twenty, a bright clear mezzo voice, quick and confident, a light American accent, cheerful and teasing, she speaks with a smile and lifts the ends of her sentences as if everything is a small adventure. A battle-worn knight commander in her forties, low and firm alto with a slight rasp, measured pace, a crisp northern English accent, stern but fair, she gives orders in short sentences and never raises her voice. A nervous goblin merchant, a thin reedy tenor that cracks when excited, very fast with sudden pauses, a sly wheedling tone, always trying to sell something, laughing nervously between words.

This step's form holds the whole wearable's settings: Slot, Layer, Route, Clearance, Cloth. Review the four views before running on: what's drawn here is what gets built. Wearable design (Qwen-Image 2.1 on the character's renders) (ultra_fast, fast, balanced, quality): Your character, rendered from four sides, is redrawn wearing the piece you describe; SAM 3.1 then finds the piece in each view by the same words, so describe it as a thing you could point at. Structure: [material and colour] → [what it is] → [length or coverage] → [one or two details]. Name one piece: 'brown leather boots', 'a steel chestplate', 'a red wool hood'. Several at once confuse the cut-out. Say how much it covers: 'knee high', 'ankle boots', 'a breastplate down to the waist'. Materials read well: leather, steel, wool, cloth, fur, gold trim. Keep it close to the body: capes, long skirts and wings need cloth simulation (not fitted yet). If SAM misses it in a view, retake with plainer words ('boots' rather than 'sabatons'). Avoid: Loose or floating parts (capes, scarves blowing, wings). Changing the character itself (hair, face): only the piece is kept. Examples: brown leather boots, knee high a steel chestplate with rivets a red wool hood leather gloves

At a glance Step id wear_mesh Used by wearable Runs built into the core (no model) Extension gen.core CLI gen retake <asset> wear_mesh --set <field>=<value> Claude Code fields, retake, look, use Builds the wearable's 3D shape by one of three routes, chosen by its words (or the Route field).

Follows the body (boots, gloves, shirts, trousers): the body's own faces inside the four masks' hull, offset by the clearance and a thickness, joined into one closed shell. It fits by construction, and leaves room over lower layers. Rigid (helmets, pauldrons, belts): Pixal3D builds it from the four views; Fit then hugs it to the body. Hanging sheet (capes): the back view's outline (filled in where the body's armour hid it) hung behind the body like a string pulled down, with folds deepening towards the hem. mesh.json records the route, why, and the pieces it was fitted over.
